1 sn In this chapter wisdom is personified. In 1:20-33 wisdom proclaims her value, and in 3:19-26 wisdom is the agent of creation. Such a personification has affinities with the wisdom literature of the ancient Near East, and may have drawn on some of that literature, albeit with appropriate safeguards (Claudia V. Camp, Wisdom and the Feminine in the Book of Proverbs, 23-70). Wisdom in Proverbs 8, however, is not a deity like Egypt&apos;s Ma`at or the Assyrian-Babylonian Ishtar. It is simply presented as if it were a self-conscious divine being distinct but subordinate to God; but in reality it is the personification of the attribute of wisdom displayed by God (R. B. Y. Scott, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes [AB], 69-72; and R. Marcus, &quot;On Biblical Hypostases of Wisdom,&quot; HUCA 23 [1950-1951]: 157-71). Many have equated wisdom in this chapter with Jesus Christ. This connection works only in so far as Jesus reveals the nature of the Father, just as Proverbs presents wisdom as an attribute of God. Jesus&apos; claims included wisdom (Matt 12:42) and a unique knowledge of God (Matt 11:25-27). He even personified wisdom in a way that was similar to Proverbs (Matt 11:19). Paul saw the fulfillment of wisdom in Christ (Col 1:15-20; 2:3) and affirmed that Christ became our wisdom in the crucifixion (1 Cor 1:24, 30). So this personification in Proverbs provides a solid foundation for the similar revelation of wisdom in Christ. But because wisdom is a creation of God in Proverbs 8, it is unlikely that wisdom here is to be identified with Jesus Christ. The chapter unfolds in three cycles: After an introduction (1-3), wisdom makes an invitation (4, 5) and explains that she is noble, just, and true (6-9); she then makes another invitation (10) and explains that she is valuable (11-21); and finally, she tells how she preceded and delights in creation (22-31) before concluding with the third invitation (32-36).

2 tn Heb &quot;head.&quot; The word רֹאשׁ (ro&apos;sh, &quot;head&quot;) refers to the highest area or most important place in the elevated area. The contrast with chapter 7 is striking. There the wayward woman lurked at the corners in the street at night; here wisdom is at the highest point in the open places in view of all. 3 tn Heb &quot;at the house of the paths.&quot; The &quot;house&quot; is not literal here, but refers to where the paths meet (cf. ASV, NIV), that is, the &quot;crossroads&quot; (so NAB, NRSV, NLT).

4 tn Heb &quot;at the mouth of.&quot; 5 tn The cry is a very loud ringing cry that could not be missed. The term רָנַן (ranan) means &quot;to give a ringing cry.&quot; It is often only a shrill sound that might come with a victory in battle, but its use in the psalms for praise shows that it also can have clear verbal content, as it does here. For wisdom to stand in the street and give such a ringing cry would mean that it could be heard by all. It was a proclamation.

1 sn Chapter 9 forms the conclusion of the lengthy introduction to the book. Both wisdom and folly will make their final appeals; and both appeal to the simpletons. Wisdom offers life with no mention of pleasure; folly offers pleasure with no mention of death. The first twelve verses concern accepting wisdom: the invitation of wisdom (1-6), the description of the responses (7-11), and the consequence (12). Verses 13-18 concern accepting folly: the invitation (13-17) and the consequence (18). 2 sn Wisdom is personified as a wise woman. She has prepared a house and established it on seven pillars. This is a reference to the habitable world (e.g., 8:31). For the equation of the house and the world, e.g., 8:29; Job 38:6; and Psalm 104:5 (also G. Boström, Proverbiastudien [LUÅ], 1-14). The &quot;seven pillars&quot; have been variously interpreted, but since seven is a number for completeness and sacredness, the idea seems to be that wisdom produced a perfect world.

3 tn Heb &quot;she has killed her killing.&quot; Cf. KJV &quot;hath killed her beasts&quot;; NAB &quot;has dressed her meat&quot;; NASB &quot;has prepared her food.&quot; 4 sn Wisdom has prepared a sumptuous banquet in this house and sends out her maids to call the simple to come and eat (M. Lichtenstein, &quot;The Banquet Motif in Keret and in Proverbs 9,&quot; JANESCU 1 [1968/69]: 19-31). The figures of meat and wine represent the good teaching of wisdom that will be palatable and profitable (implied comparisons). Compare Isaiah 55:1-2 and John 6:51, 55 for similar uses of the figures. The idea of mixing wine could refer to the practice of mixing wine with spices or with water (as the LXX text assumes; e.g., Prov 23:30; Isa 5:22). Mixed wine was the most intoxicating; thus, her wisdom is attractive. All the imagery lets the simple know that what wisdom has to offer is marvelous.
5 tn The text uses two synonymous terms in construct to express the superlative degree.

1 sn Beginning with ch. 10 there is a difference in the form of the material contained in the book of Proverbs. No longer are there long admonitions, but the actual proverbs, short aphorisms dealing with right or wrong choices. Other than a few similar themes grouped together here and there, there is no arrangement to the material as a whole. It is a long collection of approximately 400 proverbs. 2 tn Heb &quot;son.&quot; 3 tn The imperfect tense describes progressive or habitual action, translated here with an English present tense. These fit the nature of proverbs which are general maxims, and not necessarily absolutes or universal truths. One may normally expect to find what the proverb notes, and one should live according to its instructions in the light of those expectations; but one should not be surprised if from time to time there is an exception. The fact that there may be an exception does not diminish the need to live by the sayings. 4 tn Heb &quot;son.&quot; 5 tn Heb &quot;grief of his mother.&quot; The noun &quot;grief&quot; is in construct, and &quot;mother&quot; is an objective genitive. The saying declares that the consequences of wisdom or folly affects the parents.

6 tn Heb &quot;treasures of wickedness&quot; (so KJV, ASV); NASB &quot;Ill-gotten gains&quot;; TEV &quot;Wealth that you get by dishonesty.&quot; 7 sn The term &quot;righteousness&quot; here means honesty (cf. TEV). Wealth has limited value even if gained honestly; but honesty delivers from mortal danger. 8 tn Heb &quot;death.&quot; This could refer to literal death, but it is probably figurative here for mortal danger or ruin.

9 tn Heb &quot;does not allow...to go hungry.&quot; The expression &quot;The Lord does not allow the appetite of the righteous to go hungry&quot; is an example of tapeinosis - a figurative expression stated in the negative to emphasize the positive: The Lord satisfies the appetite of the righteous. 10 tn The term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) means &quot;soul&quot; but its root meaning is &quot;throat&quot; and it has a broad range of meanings; here it denotes &quot;appetite&quot; (BDB 660 s.v. 5.a; see, e.g., Pss 63:6; 107:9; Prov 27:7; Isa 56:11; 58:10; Jer 50:19; Ezek 7:19). The term could denote &quot;desire&quot; (BDB 660 s.v. 6.a) which would include the inner urge for success. By contrast, the wicked live unfulfilled lives - as far as spiritual values are concerned. 11 tn Heb &quot;thrusts away&quot; (cf. ASV, NASB); NLT &quot;refuses to satisfy.&quot; The verb הָדַף (hadaf) means &quot;to thrust away; to push; to drive,&quot; either to depose or reject (BDB 213 s.v.). 12 tn This verse contrasts the &quot;appetite&quot; of the righteous with the &quot;craving&quot; of the wicked. This word הַוַּה (havvah, &quot;craving&quot;) means &quot;desire&quot; often in a bad sense, as &apos;the desire of the wicked,&quot; which could not be wholesome (Ps 52:9).

1 tn Heb &quot;an abomination of the Lord.&quot; The term יְהוָה (yÿhvah, &quot;the Lord&quot;) is a subjective genitive. 2 tn Heb &quot;scales of deception.&quot; The genitive is attributive: &quot;deceptive scales.&quot; This refers to dishonesty in the market where silver was weighed in the scales. God condemns dishonest business practices (Deut 25:13-16; Lev 10:35-36), as did the ancient Near East (ANET 388, 423). 3 tn Heb &quot;a perfect stone.&quot; Stones were used for measuring amounts of silver on the scales; here the stone that pleases the Lord is whole, complete, perfect (from שָׁלֵם, shalem). It was one that would give an honest, accurate measurement.

4 tn Heb &quot;presumptuousness.&quot; This term is from the root זִיד, zid (or זוּד, zud) which means &quot;to boil; to seethe; to act proudly; to act presumptuously.&quot; The idea is that of boiling over the edge of the pot, signifying overstepping the boundaries (e.g., Gen 25:29). 5 tn The verbs show both the sequence and the correlation. The first is the perfect tense of בּוֹא (bo&apos;, &quot;to enter; to come&quot;); it is followed by the preterite with vav consecutive from the same verb, showing that one follows or comes with the other. Because the second verb in the colon is sequential to the first, the first may be subordinated as a temporal clause. 6 sn This proverb does not state how the disgrace will come, but affirms that it will follow pride. The proud will be brought down. 7 tn Heb &quot;modesty&quot;; KJV, ASV &quot;the lowly.&quot; The adjective צְנוּעִים (tsÿnu&apos;im, &quot;modest&quot;) is used as a noun; this is an example of antimeria in which one part of speech is used in the place of another (see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 491-506), e.g., &quot;Let the dry [adjective] appear!&quot; = dry land (Gen 1:9). The root צָנַע (tsana&apos;, &quot;to be modest; to be humble&quot;) describes those who are reserved, retiring, modest. The plural form is used for the abstract idea of humility. 8 tn The term &quot;comes&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew, but is supplied in the translation from parallelism.

9 sn This contrasts two lifestyles, affirming the value of integrity. The upright live with integrity - blamelessness - and that integrity leads them in success and happiness. Those who use treachery will be destroyed by it. 10 tc The form is a Kethib/Qere reading. The Qere יְשָׁדֵּם (yÿshadem) is an imperfect tense with the pronominal suffix. The Kethib וְשַׁדָּם (vÿshadam) is a perfect tense with a vav prefixed and a pronominal suffix. The Qere is supported by the versions.

1 tn The term &quot;accepts&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew but is supplied in the translation for the sake of smoothness and clarity. 2 tc G. R. Driver suggested reading this word as מְיֻסַּר (mÿyussar, &quot;allows himself to be disciplined&quot;); see his &quot;Hebrew Notes on Prophets and Proverbs,&quot; JTS 41 (1940): 174. But this is not necessary at all; the MT makes good sense as it stands. Similarly, the LXX has &quot;a wise son listens to his father.&quot; tn Heb &quot;discipline of a father.&quot; 3 sn The &quot;scoffer&quot; is the worst kind of fool. He has no respect for authority, reviles worship of God, and is unteachable because he thinks he knows it all. The change to a stronger word in the second colon - &quot;rebuke&quot; (גָּעַר, ga&apos;ar) - shows that he does not respond to instruction on any level. Cf. NLT &quot;a young mocker,&quot; taking this to refer to the opposite of the &quot;wise son&quot; in the first colon.

4 tn Heb &quot;lips&quot; (so NIV); KJV &quot;mouth.&quot; The term &quot;lips&quot; is a metonymy of cause for what the lips produce: speech. 5 tn Heb &quot;he eats [what is] good.&quot; 6 tn Heb &quot;the desire of the faithless.&quot; The noun &quot;faithless&quot; is a subjective genitive: &quot;the faithless desire....&quot; 7 tn The noun נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, traditionally &quot;soul&quot;) has a broad range of meanings, and here denotes &quot;appetite&quot; (e.g., Ps 17:9; Prov 23:3; Eccl 2:24; Isa 5:14; Hab 2:5; BDB 660 s.v. 5.c) or (2) &quot;desire&quot; (e.g., Deut 12:20; Prov 13:4; 19:8; 21:10; BDB 660 s.v. 6.a). 8 tn Heb &quot;violence.&quot; The phrase &quot;the fruit of&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew but is implied by the parallelism. The term &quot;violence&quot; is probably a metonymy of cause: &quot;violence&quot; represents what violence gains - ill-gotten gains resulting from violent crime. The wicked desire what does not belong to them. tc The LXX reads &quot;the souls of the wicked perish untimely.&quot; The MT makes sense as it stands.

9 tn Heb &quot;mouth&quot; (so KJV, NAB). The term פֶּה (peh, &quot;mouth&quot;) functions as a metonymy of cause for speech. 10 tn The term &quot;but&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew but is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity and smoothness. 11 tn Heb &quot;opens wide his lips.&quot; This is an idiom meaning &quot;to be talkative&quot; (BDB 832 s.v. פָּשַׂק Qal). Cf. NIV &quot;speaks rashly&quot;; TEV &quot;a careless talker&quot;; CEV &quot;talk too much.&quot; 12 sn Tight control over what one says prevents trouble (e.g., Prov 10:10; 17:28; Jas 3:1-12; Sir 28:25). Amenemope advises to &quot;sleep a night before speaking&quot; (5:15; ANET 422, n. 10). The old Arab proverb is appropriate: &quot;Take heed that your tongue does not cut your throat&quot; (O. Zockler, Proverbs, 134).

1 tn Heb &quot;wise ones of women.&quot; The construct phrase חַכְמוֹת נָשִׁים (khakhmot nashim) features a wholistic genitive: &quot;wise women.&quot; The plural functions in a distributive sense: &quot;every wise woman.&quot; The contrast is between wise and foolish women (e.g., Prov 7:10-23; 31:10-31). 2 tn The perfect tense verb in the first colon functions in a gnomic sense, while the imperfect tense in the second colon is a habitual imperfect. 3 tn Heb &quot;house.&quot; This term functions as a synecdoche of container (= house) for contents (= household, family).

4 tn Heb &quot;fear of the Lord.&quot; The term יְהוָה (yÿhvah, &quot;the Lord&quot;) functions as an objective genitive. 5 tn Heb &quot;crooked of ways&quot;; NRSV &quot;devious in conduct.&quot; This construct phrase features a genitive of specification: &quot;crooked in reference to his ways.&quot; The term &quot;ways&quot; is an idiom for moral conduct. The evidence that people fear the Lord is uprightness; the evidence of those who despise him is the devious ways.

6 tn The preposition בְּ (bet) may denote (1) exchange: &quot;in exchange for&quot; foolish talk there is a rod; or (2) cause: &quot;because of&quot; foolish talk. 7 sn The noun פֶּה (peh, &quot;mouth&quot;) functions as a metonymy of cause for what is said (&quot;speech, words, talk&quot;). 8 tc The MT reads גַּאֲוָה (ga&apos;avah, &quot;pride&quot;) which creates an awkward sense &quot;in the mouth of a fool is a rod of pride&quot; (cf. KJV, ASV). The BHS editors suggest emending the form to גֵּוֹה (&quot;disciplining-rod&quot;) to create tighter parallelism and irony: &quot;in the mouth of a fool is a rod for the back&quot; (e.g., Prov 10:13). What the fools says will bring discipline. tn Heb &quot;a rod of back.&quot; The noun גֵּוֹה functions as a genitive of specification: &quot;a rod for his back.&quot; The fool is punished because of what he says. 9 tn Heb &quot;lips.&quot; The term &quot;lips&quot; is a metonymy of cause, meaning what they say. The wise by their speech will find protection.

1 tn Heb &quot;soft answer.&quot; The adjective רַּךְ (rakh, &quot;soft; tender; gentle&quot;; BDB 940 s.v.) is more than a mild response; it is conciliatory, an answer that restores good temper and reasonableness (W. McKane, Proverbs [OTL], 477). Gideon illustrates this kind of answer (Judg 8:1-3) that brings peace. 2 tn Heb &quot;word of harshness&quot;; KJV &quot;grievous words.&quot; The noun עֶצֶב (&apos;etsev, &quot;pain, hurt&quot;) functions as an attributive genitive. The term עֶצֶב refers to something that causes pain (BDB 780 s.v. I עֶצֶב). For example, Jephthah&apos;s harsh answer led to war (Judg 12:1-6). 3 tn Heb &quot;raises anger.&quot; A common response to painful words is to let one&apos;s temper flare up.

4 sn The contrast is between the &quot;tongue of the wise&quot; and the &quot;mouth of the fool.&quot; Both expressions are metonymies of cause; the subject matter is what they say. How wise people are can be determined from what they say. 5 tn Or &quot;makes knowledge acceptable&quot; (so NASB). The verb תֵּיטִיב (tetiv, Hiphil imperfect of יָטַב [yatav, &quot;to be good&quot;]) can be translated &quot;to make good&quot; or &quot;to treat in a good [or, excellent] way&quot; (C. H. Toy, Proverbs [ICC], 303). M. Dahood, however, suggests emending the text to תֵּיטִיף (tetif) which is a cognate of נָטַף (nataf, &quot;drip&quot;), and translates &quot;tongues of the sages drip with knowledge&quot; (Proverbs and Northwest Semitic Philology, 32-33). But this change is gratuitous and unnecessary. 6 sn The Hiphil verb יַבִּיעַ (yabia&apos;) means &quot;to pour out; to emit; to cause to bubble; to belch forth.&quot; The fool bursts out with reckless utterances (cf. 7 sn The proverb uses anthropomorphic language to describe God&apos;s exacting and evaluating knowledge of all people. 8 tn The form צֹפוֹת (tsofot, &quot;watching&quot;) is a feminine plural participle agreeing with &quot;eyes.&quot; God&apos;s watching eyes comfort good people but convict evil.

The second view fits the contrast better. The proverb then is giving a glimpse of how God even confounds the wise. When someone is trying to speak [&quot;answer&quot; in the book seems to refer to a verbal answer] before others, the Lord directs the words according to his sovereign will.

6 tn Heb &quot;ways of a man.&quot; 7 sn The Hebrew term translated &quot;right&quot; (z~E) means &quot;innocent&quot; (NIV) or &quot;pure&quot; (NAB, NRSV, NLT). It is used in the Bible for pure oils or undiluted liquids; here it means unmixed actions. Therefore on the one hand people rather naively conclude that their actions are fine. 8 tn Heb &quot;in his eyes.&quot; 9 tn The figure (a hypocatastasis) of &quot;weighing&quot; signifies &quot;evaluation&quot; (e.g., Exod 5:8; 1 Sam 2:3; 16:7; Prov 21:2; 24:12). There may be an allusion to the Egyptian belief of weighing the heart after death to determine righteousness. But in Hebrew thought it is an ongoing evaluation as well, not merely an evaluation after death. 10 tn Heb &quot;spirits&quot; (so KJV, ASV). This is a metonymy for the motives, the intentions of the heart (e.g., 21:2 and 24:2). sn Humans deceive themselves rather easily and so appear righteous in their own eyes; but the proverb says that God evaluates motives and so he alone can determine if the person&apos;s ways are innocent.

11 tc The MT reads גֹּל (gol, &quot;commit&quot;) from the root גָּלַל (galal, &quot;to roll&quot;). The LXX and Tg. This would be accomplished with a spirit of humility and by means of diligent prayer, but the plan must also have God&apos;s approval. 12 tn The suffix on the plural noun would be a subjective genitive: &quot;the works you are doing,&quot; or here, &quot;the works that you want to do.&quot; 13 tn The syntax of the second clause shows that there is subordination: The vav on וְיִכֹּנוּ (vÿyikonu) coming after the imperative of the first clause expresses that this clause is the purpose or result. 1 tn The phrase &quot;a dry piece of bread&quot; is like bread without butter, a morsel of bread not dipped in vinegar mix (e.g., Ruth 2:14). It represents here a simple, humble meal. 2 tn Heb &quot;and quietness in it&quot;; the construction functions as a circumstantial clause: &quot;in which there is quietness&quot; or &quot;with quietness.&quot; sn The Hebrew word means &quot;quietness&quot; or &quot;ease.&quot; It represents a place where there can be carefree ease because of the sense of peace and security. The Greek rendering suggests that those translators read it as &quot;peace.&quot; Even if the fare is poor, this kind of setting is to be preferred. 3 tn The house is described as being full of &quot;sacrifices of strife&quot; (זִבְחֵי־רִיב, zivkhi-riv). The use of &quot;sacrifices&quot; suggests a connection with the temple (as in 7:14) in which the people may have made their sacrifices and had a large amount meat left over. It is also possible that the reference is simply to a sumptuous meal (Deut 12:15; Isa 34:6; Ezek 39:17). It would be rare for Israelites to eat meat apart from festivals, however. In the construction the genitive could be classified as a genitive of effect, the feast in general &quot;bringing about strife,&quot; or it could simply be an attributive genitive, &quot;a feast characterized by strife.&quot; Abundance often brings deterioration of moral and ethical standards as well as an increase in envy and strife.

4 sn The setting is in the ancient world where a servant rarely advanced beyond his or her station in life. But there are notable exceptions (e.g., Gen 15:3 where the possibility is mentioned, 1 Chr 2:35 where it changed through marriage, and 2 Sam 16:1-4; 19:24-30, with the story of Ziba the servant of Mephibosheth). This proverb focuses on a servant who is wise, one who uses all his abilities effectively - a Joseph figure. 5 sn The parallelism indicates that &quot;ruling over&quot; and &quot;sharing in the inheritance&quot; means that the disgraceful son will be disinherited. 6 tn Heb &quot;son.&quot; 7 tn The form מֵבִישׁ (mevish) is a Hiphil participle, modifying בֵן (ben). This original heir would then be one who caused shame or disgrace to the family, probably by showing a complete lack of wisdom in the choices he made. 8 tn Heb &quot;in the midst of the brothers&quot;; NIV &quot;as one of the brothers.&quot;

9 sn The noun מַצְרֵף (matsref) means &quot;a place or instrument for refining&quot; (cf. ASV, NASB &quot;the refining pot&quot;). The related verb, which means &quot;to melt, refine, smelt,&quot; is used in scripture literally for refining and figuratively for the Lord&apos;s purifying and cleansing and testing people. 10 tn The term &quot;refining&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the parallelism; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 11 sn The term כּוּר (cur) describes a &quot;furnace&quot; or &quot;smelting pot.&quot; It can be used figuratively for the beneficial side of affliction (Isa 48:10). 12 tn Heb &quot;and.&quot; Most English versions treat this as an adversative (&quot;but&quot;). 13 sn The participle בֹּחֵן (bokhen, &quot;tests&quot;) in this emblematic parallelism takes on the connotations of the crucible and the furnace. When the Lord &quot;tests&quot; human hearts, the test, whatever form it takes, is designed to improve the value of the one being tested. Evil and folly will be removed when such testing takes place.

1 sn People should follow honesty even if it leads to poverty (e.g., Prov 18:23; 19:22). 2 tn Heb &quot;lips.&quot; The term &quot;lips&quot; is a metonymy for what one says with his lips. The expression &quot;perverse in his lips&quot; refers to speech that is morally perverted. Some medieval Hebrew mss, the Syriac, and Tg. Prov 19:1 have &quot;his ways&quot; rather than &quot;his lips&quot; (e.g., Prov 28:6); cf. NAB. 3 tc The Syriac and Tg. Prov 19:1 read &quot;rich&quot; instead of MT &quot;fool.&quot; This makes tighter antithetical parallelism than MT and is followed by NAB. However, the MT makes sense as it stands; this is an example of metonymical parallelism. The MT reading is also supported by the LXX. The Hebrew construction uses וְהוּא (vÿhu&apos;), &quot;and he [is],&quot; before &quot;fool.&quot; This may be rendered &quot;one who is perverse while a fool&quot; or &quot;a fool at the same time.&quot;

4 tn Heb &quot;not good.&quot; This is a figure known as tapeinosis (a deliberate understatement to emphasize a worst-case scenario): &quot;it is dangerous!&quot; 5 tn The interpretation of this line depends largely on the meaning of נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) which has a broad range of meanings: (1) the breathing substance of man, (2) living being, (3) life, (4) person, (5) seat of the appetites, (6) seat of emotions and passions, (7) activities of intellect, emotion and will, (8) moral character, etc. (BDB 659-61 s.v.). In light of the synonymous parallelism, the most likely nuance here is &quot;zeal, passion&quot; (HALOT 713 s.v. 8). NIV takes the word in the sense of &quot;vitality&quot; and &quot;drive&quot; - &quot;it is not good to have zeal without knowledge&quot; (cf. NCV, TEV, and NLT which are all similar). 6 tn Heb &quot;he who is hasty with his feet.&quot; The verb אוּץ (&apos;uts) means &quot;to be pressed; to press; to make haste.&quot; The verb is followed by the preposition בְּ (bet) which indicates that with which one hastens - his feet. The word &quot;feet&quot; is a synecdoche of part for the whole person - body and mind working together (cf. NLT &quot;a person who moves too quickly&quot;). 7 tn Heb &quot;misses the goal.&quot; The participle חוֹטֵא (khote&apos;) can be translated &quot;sins&quot; (cf. KJV, ASV), but in this context it refers only to actions without knowledge, which could lead to sin, or could lead simply to making poor choices (cf. NAB &quot;blunders&quot;; NASB &quot;errs&quot;; NCV &quot;might make a mistake&quot;). sn The basic meaning of the verb is &quot;to miss a goal or the way.&quot; D. Kidner says, &quot;How negative is the achievement of a man who wants tangible and quick rewards&quot; - he will miss the way (Proverbs [TOTC], 132).

8 tn Heb &quot;the folly of a man.&quot; 9 tn The verb סָלַף (salaf) normally means &quot;to twist; to pervert; to overturn,&quot; but in this context it means &quot;to subvert&quot; (BDB 701 s.v.); cf. ASV &quot;subverteth.&quot; sn J. H. Greenstone comments: &quot;Man&apos;s own failures are the result of his own folly and should not be attributed to God&quot; (Proverbs, 201). 10 tn The clause begins with vav on the nonverb phrase &quot;against the Lord.&quot; While clause structure and word order is less compelling in a book like Proverbs, this fits well as a circumstantial clause indicating concession. 11 sn The &quot;heart raging&quot; is a metonymy of cause (or adjunct); it represents the emotions that will lead to blaming God for the frustration. Genesis 42:28 offers a calmer illustration of this as the brothers ask what God was doing to them.

1 sn The drinks are wine and barley beer (e.g., Lev 10:9; Deut 14:26; Isa 28:7). These terms here could be understood as personifications, but better as metonymies for those who drink wine and beer. The inebriated person mocks and brawls. 2 tn The two participles לֵץ (lets, &quot;mocker&quot;) and הֹמֶה (homeh, &quot;brawler&quot;) are substantives; they function as predicates in the sentence. Excessive use of intoxicants excites the drinker to boisterous behavior and aggressive attitudes - it turns them into mockers and brawlers. 3 sn The proverb does not prohibit the use of wine or beer; in fact, strong drink was used at festivals and celebrations. But intoxication was considered out of bounds for a member of the covenant community (e.g., 23:20-21, 29-35; 31:4-7). To be led astray by their use is not wise.

4 tn Heb &quot;the terror of a king&quot; (so ASV, NASB); The term &quot;terror&quot; is a metonymy of effect for cause: the anger of a king that causes terror among the people. The term &quot;king&quot; functions as a possessive genitive: &quot;a king&apos;s anger&quot; (cf. NIV &quot;A king&apos;s wrath&quot;; NLT &quot;The king&apos;s fury&quot;). 5 tn The verb מִתְעַבְּרוֹ (mit&apos;abbÿro) is problematic; in the MT the form is the Hitpael participle with a pronominal suffix, which is unusual, for the direct object of this verb usually takes a preposition first: &quot;is angry with.&quot; The LXX rendered it &quot;angers [or, irritates].&quot; 6 sn The expression &quot;sins against himself&quot; has been taken by some to mean &quot;forfeits his life&quot; (so NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV) or &quot;endangers his life&quot; (cf. NCV, NLT). That may be the implication of getting oneself in trouble with an angry king (cf. TEV &quot;making him angry is suicide&quot;).

7 tn Heb &quot;man.&quot; 8 tn Heb &quot;cessation&quot; (שֶׁבֶת, shevet); NAB &quot;to shun strife&quot;; NRSV &quot;refrain from strife.&quot; sn One cannot avoid conflict altogether; but the proverb is instructing that at the first sign of conflict the honorable thing to do is to find a way to end it. 9 tn Heb &quot;breaks out.&quot; The Hitpael of the verb גָּלַע (gala&apos;, &quot;to expose; to lay bare&quot;) means &quot;to break out; to disclose oneself,&quot; and so the idea of flaring up in a quarrel is clear. 1 tn Heb &quot;a name.&quot; The idea of the name being &quot;good&quot; is implied; it has the connotation here of a reputation (cf. TEV, CEV, NLT). 2 tn &quot;To be chosen rather than&quot; is a translation of the Niphal participle with the comparative degree taken into consideration. Cf. CEV &quot;worth much more than.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;favor of goodness.&quot; This is a somewhat difficult expression. Some English versions render the phrase &quot;favor is better than silver or gold&quot; (so NASB, NRSV) making it parallel to the first colon. But if &quot;good&quot; is retained as an attributive modifier, then it would mean one was well thought of, or one had engaging qualities (cf. ASV &quot;loving favor; NLT &quot;high esteem&quot;). This fits with the idea of the reputation in the first colon, for a good name would bring with it the favor of others.

4 tn The form of the verb is the Niphal perfect of פָּגַשׁ (pagash); it means &quot;to meet together [or, each other]&quot; (cf. KJV, ASV). The point is that rich and poor live side by side in this life, but they are both part of God&apos;s creation (cf. NAB, NASB &quot;have a common bond&quot;). Some commentators have taken this to mean that they should live together because they are part of God&apos;s creation; but the verb form will not sustain that meaning. 5 tn Heb &quot;all.&quot; The Lord is sovereign over both groups, that is, he has had the final say whether a person is rich or poor. People would do well to treat all people with respect, for God can as easily reduce the rich to poverty as raise up the poor to wealth.

6 sn The contrast is between the &quot;shrewd&quot; (prudent) person and the &quot;simpleton.&quot; The shrewd person knows where the dangers and pitfalls are in life and so can avoid them; the naive person is unwary, untrained, and gullible, unable to survive the dangers of the world and blundering into them. 7 tn Heb &quot;evil,&quot; a term that is broad enough to include (1) &quot;sin&quot; as well as (2) any form of &quot;danger&quot; (NIV, NCV, NRSV, NLT) or &quot;trouble&quot; (TEV, CEV). The second option is more likely what is meant here: The naive simpleton does not see the danger to be avoided and so suffers for it. 8 tn Heb &quot;go on&quot;; the word &quot;right&quot; is supplied in the translation to clarify the meaning: The naive person, oblivious to impending danger, meets it head on (cf. TEV &quot;will walk right into it&quot;). 9 tn The verb עָנַשׁ (&apos;anash) means &quot;to fine&quot; specifically. In the Niphal stem it means &quot;to be fined,&quot; or more generally, &quot;to be punished.&quot; In this line the punishment is the consequence of blundering into trouble - they will pay for it.

1 tn The construction uses the imperfect tense of instruction with the infinitive absolute to emphasize the careful discernment required on such occasions. Cf. NIV &quot;note well&quot;; NLT &quot;pay attention.&quot; 2 tn Or &quot;who,&quot; referring to the ruler (so ASV, NAB, TEV).

3 sn The expression &quot;put a knife to your throat&quot; is an idiom that means &quot;curb your appetite&quot; or &quot;control yourself&quot; (cf. TEV). The instruction was from a time when people dealt with all-powerful tyrants. To enter the presence of such a person and indulge one&apos;s appetites would be to take a very high risk. 4 tn Heb &quot;lord of appetite.&quot; The idiom בַּעַל נֶפֶשׁ (ba&apos;al nefesh) refers to someone who possesses a large appetite (cf. NAB &quot;a ravenous appetite&quot;). A person with a big appetite is in danger of taking liberties when invited to court.

5 tn Heb &quot;his&quot;; the referent (the ruler mentioned in v. 1) has been specified in the translation for clarity. 6 sn The final line gives the causal clause: The impressive feast is not what it appears to be; the king is not doing you a favor, but rather wants something from you or is observing you (K&D 17:104); cf. TEV &quot;he may be trying to trick you.&quot; 7 sn Verses 1-3 form the sixth saying about being cautious before rulers (cf. Instruction of Amememope, chap. 23, 23:13-18). One should not get too familiar with rulers, for they always have ulterior motives. The Mishnah cites Gamaliel as warning that a ruler only draws someone into his court for his purpose, but in their day of trouble he will not be there to help them (m. Abot 2:3).

1 sn This section of the book of Proverbs contains proverbs attributed to Solomon but copied by Hezekiah&apos;s sages (between 715 b.c. and 687 b.c.). Some scholars conclude that this has no historical value other than to report the later disposition that people thought they came from Solomon&apos;s time, but if that were the only consideration, then that in itself would have to be considered as a piece of historical information. But if the reference is an earlier note in the collection, then it becomes more valuable for consideration. The proverbs in these lines differ from the earlier ones in that these are multiple line sayings using more similes; chapters 28-29 are similar to 10-16, but chapters 25-27 differ in having few references to God.

2 sn The proverb provides a contrast between God and the king, and therein is the clue to the range of application involved. The interest of the king is ruling or administering his government; and so the subject matter is a contrast to the way God rules his kingdom. 3 sn The two infinitives form the heart of the contrast - &quot;to conceal a matter&quot; and &quot;to search out a matter.&quot; God&apos;s government of the universe is beyond human understanding - humans cannot begin to fathom the intentions and operations of it. But it is the glory of kings to search out matters and make them intelligible to the people. Human government cannot claim divine secrecy; kings have to study and investigate everything before making a decision, even divine government as far as possible. But kings who rule as God&apos;s representatives must also try to represent his will in human affairs - they must even inquire after God to find his will. This is their glorious nature and responsibility. For more general information on vv. 2-27, see G. E. Bryce, &quot;Another Wisdom &apos;Book&apos; in Proverbs,&quot; JBL 91 (1972): 145-57.

4 tn Heb &quot;heavens for height and earth for depth.&quot; The proverb is clearly intending the first line to be an illustration of the second - it is almost emblematic parallelism. 5 sn The proverb is affirming a simple fact: The king&apos;s plans and decisions are beyond the comprehension of the common people. While the king would make many things clear to the people, there are other things that are &quot;above their heads&quot; or &quot;too deep for them.&quot; They are unsearchable because of his superior wisdom, his caprice, or his need for secrecy. Inscrutability is sometimes necessary to keep a firm grip on power.

1 sn &quot;Honor&quot; in this passage probably means respect, external recognition of worth, accolades, advancement to high position, etc. All of these would be out of place with a fool; so the sage is warning against elevating or acclaiming those who are worthless. See also J. A. Emerton, &quot;Notes on Some Passages in the Book of Proverbs,&quot; VT 15 (1965): 271-79. 2 sn The first twelve verses of this chapter, Prov 26:1-12, are sometimes called &quot;the Book of Fools&quot; because they deal with the actions of fools.

3 tn Heb &quot;causeless curse&quot; (KJV similar) describes an undeserved curse (cf. NIV, NRSV). The Hebrew word translated &quot;causeless&quot; is the adverb from ָחנַן (khanan); it means &quot;without cause; gratuitous.&quot; sn This proverb is saying that a curse that is uttered will be powerless if that curse is undeserved. It was commonly believed in the ancient world that blessings and curses had power in themselves, that once spoken they were effectual. But scripture makes it clear that the power of a blessing or a curse depends on the power of the one behind it (e.g., Num 22:38; 23:8). A curse would only take effect if the one who declared it had the authority to do so, and he would only do that if the curse was deserved. 4 tc The MT has the negative with the verb &quot;to enter; to come&quot; to mean &quot;will not come&quot; (לֹא תָבֹא, lo&apos; tavo&apos;). This is interpreted to mean &quot;will not come to rest&quot; or &quot;will not come home.&quot; Some commentators have taken the Qere reading of לוֹ (lo) instead, and read it as &quot;will come home to him.&quot; This is also a little difficult; but it gives the idea that an undeserved curse will come [back] to him [who gave it]. Just as a bird will fly around and eventually come home, so will the undeserved curse return on the one who gave it. This is plausible; but there is no referent for the suffix, making it syntactically difficult.
5 sn A fool must be disciplined by force like an animal - there is no reasoning. The fool is as difficult to manage as the donkey or horse.

1 tn The form אַל־תִּתְהַלֵּל (&apos;al-tithallel) is the Hitpael jussive negated; it is from the common verb &quot;to praise,&quot; and so in this setting means &quot;to praise oneself&quot; or &quot;to boast.&quot; sn The verse rules out one&apos;s overconfident sense of ability to control the future. No one can presume on the future. 2 sn The word &quot;tomorrow&quot; is a metonymy of subject, meaning what will be done tomorrow, or in the future in general. 3 sn The expression &quot;you do not know&quot; balances the presumption of the first line, reminding the disciple of his ignorance and therefore his need for humility (e.g., Matt 6:34; Luke 12:20; Jas 4:13-16).

4 tn Heb &quot;a stranger.&quot; This does not necessarily refer to a non-Israelite, as has been demonstrated before in the book of Proverbs, but these are people outside the familiar and accepted circles. The point is that such a person would be objective in speaking about your abilities and accomplishments. 5 sn &quot;Mouth&quot; and &quot;lips&quot; are metonymies of cause; they mean &quot;what is said.&quot; People should try to avoid praising themselves. Self praise can easily become a form of pride, even if it begins with trivial things. It does not establish a reputation; reputation comes from what others think about you. 6 tn &quot;a foreigner&quot;; KJV, ASV, NASB, NRSV &quot;a stranger.&quot;

7 tn The subject matter is the vexation produced by a fool. The term כַּעַס (ca&apos;as) means &quot;vexation&quot; (ASV); provocation&quot; (NAB, NASB, NIV, NRSV); &quot;anger&quot; (KJV &quot;wrath&quot;) and usually refers to undeserved treatment. Cf. NLT &quot;the resentment caused by a fool.&quot; sn The same noun is used in 1 Sam 1:6, 16 for the &quot;provocation&quot; given to Hannah by Peninnah for being barren. 8 sn The contrast is made between dealing with the vexation of a fool and physical labor (moving stones and sand). 1 sn The line portrays the insecurity of a guilty person - he flees because he has a guilty conscience, or because he is suspicious of others around him, or because he fears judgment. 2 tn The verb בָּטַח (batakh) means &quot;to trust; to be secure; to be confident.&quot; Cf. KJV, NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT &quot;bold.&quot; sn The righteous, who seek to find favor with God and man, have a clear conscience and do not need to look over their shoulders for avengers or law enforcers. Their position is one of confidence, so that they do not flee.

3 sn The Hebrew word translated &quot;rebellious&quot; has rebellion as its basic meaning, and that is the idea here. The proverb is describing a time when sinfulness brings about social and political unrest. 4 tn Heb &quot;many are its princes&quot; (so NASB). sn In such a chaotic time there will be many rulers, either simultaneously or in a rapid sequence. The times of the judges or the days of the northern kings of Israel provide examples. 5 tn Heb &quot;a man who understands [and] knows&quot;; NRSV &quot;an intelligent ruler&quot;; NLT &quot;wise and knowledgeable leaders.&quot; 6 tc The LXX reads (probably from a different underlying Hebrew text): &quot;It is the fault of a violent man that quarrels start, but they are settled by a man of discernment.&quot; For a survey of suggestions, see C. H. Toy, Proverbs (ICC), 495, and W. McKane, Proverbs (OTL), 630. tn This last line is difficult. The MT has כֵּן יַאֲרִיךְ (ken ya&apos;arikh). The verb means &quot;to prolong,&quot; but כֵּן (ken) is open to several possibilities for meaning. J. H. Greenstone&apos;s interpretation of it as a noun from the Hollow root כּוּן (kun) with a meaning of &quot;established order&quot; is what is expected here (Proverbs, 293). sn For a study of the verses in chapters 28 and 29 concerning kings and governments, see B. V. Malchow, &quot;A Manual for Future Monarchs,&quot; CBQ 47 (1985): 238-45.

7 tc The MT reads &quot;a poor man,&quot; גֶּבֶר רָשׁ (gever rash); cf. KJV, NASB, NLT. The problem is that the poor in the book of Proverbs is not an oppressor and does not have the power to be such. So commentators assume the word is incorrect. By a slight change to רָשָׁע (rasha&apos;) the reading becomes &quot;a wicked ruler&quot; [Heb &quot;a wicked mighty man&quot;]. There is no textual support for this change. The LXX, however, reads, &quot;A courageous man oppresses the poor with impieties.&quot; If &quot;a poor man&quot; is retained, then the oppression would include betrayal - one would expect a poor man to have sympathy for others who are impoverished, but in fact that is not the case. It is a sad commentary on human nature that the truly oppressed people can also be oppressed by other poor people. 8 tn The comparative &quot;like&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the metaphor; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 9 sn &quot;Food&quot; is a metonymy of effect here. The picture is of the driving rain that should cause crops to grow so that food can be produced - but does not (some English versions assume the crops are destroyed instead, e.g., NCV, TEV, CEV, NLT). The point the proverb is making is that a show of strength may not produce anything except ruin.

1 tn The idiom &quot;to harden the neck&quot; (מַקְשֶׁה־עֹרֶף, maqsheh-&apos;oref) is the idea of resisting the rebukes and persisting in obstinacy (e.g., Exod 32:9). The opposite of a &quot;stiff neck&quot; would be the bending back, i.e., submission. 2 tn The Hebrew construction is אִישׁ תּוֹכָחוֹת (&apos;ish tokhakhot, &quot;a man of rebukes&quot;), meaning &quot;a man who has (or receives) many rebukes.&quot; This describes a person who is deserving of punishment and who has been given many warnings. The text says, then, &quot;a man of rebukes hardening himself.&quot; 3 sn The stubborn person refuses to listen; he will suddenly be destroyed when the calamity strikes (e.g., Prov 6:15; 13:18; 15:10). 4 tn Or &quot;healing&quot; (NRSV).

5 tn The Hebrew form בִּרְבוֹת (birvot) is the Qal infinitive construct of רָבָה (ravah) with a בּ (bet) preposition, forming a temporal clause with a subjective genitive following it. It is paralleled in the second colon by the same construction, showing the antithesis: וּבִמְשֹׁל (uvimshol), &quot;and when the wicked rule.&quot; Some commentators wish to change the first verb to make it parallel this more closely, e.g., רָדָה (radah, &quot;to rule&quot;), but that would be too neat and is completely unsupported. The contrast is between when the righteous increase and when the wicked rule. It is not hard to see how this contrast works out in society. 6 tn The Niphal verb אָנַח (&apos;anakh) means &quot;to sigh; to groan,&quot; usually because of grief or physical and emotional distress. The word is a metonymy of effect; the cause is the oppression and distress due to evil rulers.

7 tn Heb &quot;a man.&quot; Here &quot;man&quot; is retained in the translation because the second colon mentions prostitutes. 8 tn Or &quot;causes his father to rejoice&quot;; NAB &quot;makes his father glad.&quot; 9 tn The active participle רֹעֶה (ro&apos;eh) is from the second root רָעָה (ra&apos;ah), meaning &quot;to associate with.&quot; The verb occurs only a few times, and mostly in the book of Proverbs. It is related to רֵעֶה (re&apos;eh, &quot;friend; companion; fellow&quot;). To describe someone as a &quot;companion&quot; or &quot;friend&quot; of prostitutes is somewhat euphemistic; it surely means someone who is frequently engaging the services of prostitutes. 10 tn The Hebrew verb יְאַבֶּד (yÿ&apos;abbed) means &quot;destroys&quot;; it is the Piel imperfect of the verb that means &quot;to perish.&quot; 11 sn Wealth was seen as a sign of success and of God&apos;s blessings, pretty much as it always has been. To be seen as honorable in the community meant one had acquired some substance and kept his reputation. It would be a disgrace to the family to have a son who squandered his money on prostitutes (e.g., Prov 5:10; 6:31).

1 sn This chapter has a title (30:1), Agur&apos;s confession and petition (30:2-9), and a series of Agur&apos;s admonitions (30:10-33). 2 tn The title הַמַּשָּׂא (hammasa&apos;) means &quot;the burden,&quot; a frequently used title in prophetic oracles. It may be that the word is a place name, although it is more likely that it describes what follows as an important revelation. 3 tn The definite article is used here as a demonstrative, clarifying the reference to Agur. 4 sn The word translated &quot;says&quot; (נְאֻם, nÿ&apos;um) is a verbal noun; it is also a term that describes an oracle. It is usually followed by the subjective genitive: &quot;the oracle of this man to Ithiel.&quot; 5 tn There have been numerous attempts to reinterpret the first two verses of the chapter. The Greek version translated the names &quot;Ithiel&quot; and &quot;Ukal,&quot; resulting in &quot;I am weary, O God, I am weary and faint&quot; (C. C. Torrey, &quot;Proverbs Chapter 30,&quot; JBL 73 [1954]: 93-96). The LXX&apos;s approach is followed by some English versions (e.g., NRSV, NLT). The Midrash tried through a clever etymologizing translation to attribute the works to Solomon (explained by W. G. Plaut, Proverbs, 299). It is most likely that someone other than Solomon wrote these sayings; they have a different, almost non-proverbial, tone to them. See P. Franklyn, &quot;The Sayings of Agur in Proverbs 30: Piety or Skepticism,&quot; ZAW 95 (1983): 239-52.

6 tn The particle כִּי (ki) functions in an asseverative sense, &quot;surely; indeed; truly&quot; (R. J. Williams, Hebrew Syntax, 73, §449). 7 tn The noun בַּעַר (ba&apos;ar) means &quot;brutishness&quot;; here it functions as a predicate adjective. It is followed by מֵאִישׁ (me&apos;ish) expressing comparative degree: &quot;more than a man&quot; or &quot;more than any man,&quot; with &quot;man&quot; used in a generic sense. He is saying that he has fallen beneath the level of mankind. Cf. NRSV &quot;I am too stupid to be human.&quot; 8 tn Heb &quot;than man.&quot; The verse is using hyperbole; this individual feels as if he has no intelligence at all, that he is more brutish than any other human. Of course this is not true, or he would not be able to speculate on the God of the universe at all. 9 tn Heb &quot;the understanding of a man,&quot; with &quot;man&quot; used attributively here.

10 sn The construction uses repetition to make the point emphatically: &quot;I do not know the knowledge of the Holy One.&quot; Agur&apos;s claim to being &quot;brutish&quot; is here clarified - he is not one of those who has knowledge or understanding of God. C. H. Toy thinks the speaker is being sarcastic in reference to others who may have claimed such knowledge (Proverbs [ICC], 521). 11 tn The epithet &quot;the Holy One&quot; is the adjective &quot;holy&quot; put in the masculine plural (as in 9:10). This will harmonize with the plural of majesty used to explain the plural with titles for God. However, NRSV takes the plural as a reference to the &quot;holy ones,&quot; presumably referring to angelic beings.

1 sn Nothing else is known about King Lemuel aside from this mention in the book of Proverbs. Jewish legend identifies him as Solomon, making this advice from his mother Bathsheba; but there is no evidence for that. The passage is the only direct address to a king in the book of Proverbs - something that was the norm in wisdom literature of the ancient world (Leah L. Brunner, &quot;King and Commoner in Proverbs and Near Eastern Sources,&quot; Dor le Dor 10 [1982]: 210-19; Brunner argues that the advice is religious and not secular). 2 tn Some English versions take the Hebrew noun translated &quot;oracle&quot; here as a place name specifying the kingdom of King Lemuel; cf. NAB &quot;king of Massa&quot;; CEV &quot;King Lemuel of Massa.&quot;

3 tn The form מַה (mah), normally the interrogative &quot;what?&quot; (so KJV, ASV, NAB, NASB) is best interpreted here as an exclamation. Tg. Prov 31:2 has &quot;Woe!&quot; 4 tn In all three occurrences in this verse the word &quot;son&quot; has the Aramaic spelling, ַַבּר (bar), rather than the Hebrew בֵּן (ben). The repetition of the word &quot;son&quot; shows the seriousness of the warning; and the expression &quot;son of my womb&quot; and &quot;son of my vows&quot; are endearing epithets to show the great investment she has made in his religious place in God&apos;s program. For a view that &quot;son of my womb&quot; should be &quot;my own son,&quot; see F. Deist, &quot;Proverbs 31:1, A Case of Constant Mistranslation,&quot; JNSL 6 (1978): 1-3; cf. TEV &quot;my own dear son.&quot;

5 sn The word translated &quot;strength&quot; refers to physical powers here, i.e., &quot;vigor&quot; (so NAB) or &quot;stamina.&quot; It is therefore a metonymy of cause; the effect would be what spending this strength meant - sexual involvement with women. It would be easy for a king to spend his energy enjoying women, but that would be unwise. 6 sn The word &quot;ways&quot; may in general refer to the heart&apos;s affection for or attention to, or it may more specifically refer to sexual intercourse. While in the book of Proverbs the term is an idiom for the course of life, in this context it must refer to the energy spent in this activity. 7 tn The construction uses Qal infinitive construct לַמְחוֹת (lamkhot, &quot;to wipe out; to blot out; to destroy&quot;). The construction is somewhat strange, and so some interpreters suggest changing it to מֹחוֹת (mokhot, &quot;destroyers of kings&quot;); cf. BDB 562 s.v. מָחָה Qal.3. Commentators note that the form is close to an Aramaic word that means &quot;concubine,&quot; and an Arabic word that is an indelicate description for women.
