172.content: 1 tn The Hebrew noun translated &quot;proverb&quot; is derived from the root מָשַׁל (mashal) which means &quot;likeness.&quot; The related Niphal verb means &quot;to be like, be comparable with,&quot; e.g., &quot;he is like [נִמְשַׁל, nimshal] the beasts that perish&quot; (Ps 49:12). The noun can mean an object lesson based on or using a comparison or analogy. It may be a short pithy statement (Ezek 16:44), object lesson drawn from experience (Ps 78:2-6), saying or by-word (Deut 28:37) or an oracle of future blessing (Ezek 21:1-5). Here it means an object lesson setting out courses of action. It helps one choose the course of action to follow or avoid. 2 tn The name שְׁלֹמֹה (shÿlomoh, &quot;of Solomon&quot;) is a genitive of authorship or source. While Solomon wrote a majority of the proverbial sayings in the book, some proverbial sayings were written by others (e.g., 22:17-24:34; 30:1-33; 31:1-9) and perhaps collected by Solomon. The name also forms a phonetic wordplay on the similarly sounding word מִשְׁלֵי (mishley, &quot;proverbs&quot;), as if to say the name is almost synonymous with proverbs. 3 sn The phrase &quot;The Proverbs of Solomon&quot; is a title for the entire book. The title does not imply that Solomon authored all the proverbs in this collection; some sections are collections from different authors: the sayings of the wise (22:17-24:22), more sayings of the wise (24:23-34), the words of Agur (Prov 30:1-33) and Lemuel (Prov 31:1-9). The title does not imply that the book was in its final canonical form in the days of Solomon; the men of Hezekiah added a collection of Solomonic proverbs to the existing form of the book (25:1-29:27). The original collection of Solomonic proverbs appears to be the collection of short pithy sayings in 10:1-22:16, and the title might have originally introduced only these. There is question whether chapters 1-9 were part of the original form of the book in the days of Solomon because they do not fit under the title; they are not &quot;proverbs&quot; per se (sentence sayings) but introductory admonitions (longer wisdom speeches). Chapters 1-9 could have been written by Solomon and perhaps added later by someone else. Or they could have been written by someone else and added later in the days of Hezekiah. 4 tn The designation &quot;son of David&quot; is in apposition to the name Solomon, as are the following nouns, further explaining the name. 5 tn The phrase &quot;the king of Israel&quot; is in apposition to the name Solomon.

6 tn The infinitive construct + ל (lamed) here designates purpose. This is the first of five purpose clauses in the opening section (1:2a, 2b, 3a, 4a, 6a). This clause reveals the purpose of the collection of proverbs in general. The three purpose clauses that follow qualify this general purpose. 7 tn Heb &quot;to know.&quot; The verb יָדַע (yada&apos;) here means &quot;to gain knowledge of&quot; or &quot;to become wise in&quot; (BDB 394 s.v. 5). This term refers to experiential knowledge, not just cognitive knowledge; it includes the intellectual assimilation and practical use of what is acquired. 8 sn The noun &quot;wisdom&quot; (חָכְמָה, khokhmah) could be nuanced &quot;moral skill.&quot; It refers to &quot;skill&quot; that produces something of value. It is used in reference to the skill of seamen (Ps 107:27), abilities of weavers (Exod 35:26), capabilities of administrators (1 Kgs 3:28), or skill of craftsmen (Exod 31:6). In the realm of moral living, it refers to skill in living - one lives life with moral skill so that something of lasting value is produced from one&apos;s life. 9 tn Heb &quot;instruction.&quot; The noun מוּסָר (musar) has a three-fold range of meanings: (1) physical or parental: &quot;discipline; chastisement&quot; (2) verbal: &quot;warning; exhortation&quot; and (3) moral: &quot;training; instruction&quot; (BDB 416 s.v. מוּסָר; HALOT 557 s.v. מוּסָר). Its parallelism with חָכְמָה (khokhmah, &quot;wisdom, moral skill&quot;) suggests that it refers to moral training or instruction that the Book of Proverbs offers to its readers. This instruction consists of wisdom acquired by observing the consequences of foolish actions in others and developing the ability to control the natural inclination to folly. This sometimes comes through experiencing chastisement from God. Sensing something of this nuance, the LXX translated this term with the Greek word for &quot;child-training.&quot; 10 tn The infinitive construct + ל (lamed) here designates a second purpose of the book: to compare and to make proper evaluation of the sayings of the wise. The term בִין (bin, &quot;to discern&quot;) refers to the ability to make distinctions between things. This is illustrated by its derivatives: The related preposition means &quot;between&quot; and the related noun means &quot;space between.&quot; So the verb refers to the ability to discern between moral options. 11 tn Heb &quot;words of discernment.&quot; The noun בִינָה (binah, &quot;discernment&quot;) functions as an attributive genitive: &quot;discerning words&quot; or &quot;wise sayings&quot; (so NLT). This noun is a cognate accusative of the infinitive of the same root לְהָבִין (lÿhavin, &quot;to discern&quot;). The phrase &quot;to discern words of discernment&quot; refers to the ability (1) to distinguish truth from falsehood or (2) to understand wise sayings, such as in Proverbs.

12 tn The infinitive construct + ל (lamed) here designates a further purpose of the book: This focuses on the purpose of the book from the perspective of the student/disciple. The verb לָקַח (laqakh, &quot;receive&quot;) means to acquire something worth having. It is parallel to the verb &quot;treasure up&quot; in 2:1. 13 tn Heb &quot;instruction.&quot; See note on the same term in 1:2. 14 tc MT reads the genitive-construct phrase מוּסַר הַשְׂכֵּל (musar haskel, &quot;discipline of prudence&quot;). Syriac adds vav (ו) and reads מוּסַר וְהַשְׂכֵּל (musar wÿhaskel, &quot;discipline and prudence&quot;). MT is the more difficult reading in terms of syntax, so is preferred as the original reading. tn Heb &quot;discipline of prudence.&quot; The term הַשְׂכֵּל (haskel, &quot;of prudence&quot;) is a Hiphil infinitive absolute, functioning as an emphatic genitive of result, describing the results of a self-disciplined life. The basic meaning of שָׂכַל is &quot;to be prudent, circumspect,&quot; and the Hiphil stem means &quot;to give attention to, consider, ponder; have insight, understanding&quot; (BDB 968 s.v. I שָׂכַל). It is a synonym of חָכְמָה (khokhmah, &quot;wisdom&quot;), but while חָכְמָה focuses on living skillfully, שָׂכַל (sakhal) focuses on acting prudently. The word can also focus on the results of acting prudently: to have success (e.g., Isa 52:12). Elsewhere, the term describes the prudent actions of Abigail in contrast to her foolish husband Nabal (1 Sam 25). 15 tn Heb &quot;righteousness and justice and equity.&quot; The three nouns that follow &quot;self-discipline of prudence&quot; are adverbial accusatives of manner, describing the ways in which the disciplined prudent activity will be manifested: &quot;in righteousness, justice, and equity.&quot; The term &quot;in&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the syntax; it is inserted in the translation for clarity. 16 sn The word &quot;righteousness&quot; (צֶדֶק, tsedeq) describes conduct that conforms to a standard. Elsewhere it is used in a concrete sense to refer to commercial weights and measures that conform to a standard (Deut 25:15). In the moral realm it refers to &quot;righteous&quot; conduct that conforms to God&apos;s law. 17 tn Heb &quot;and justice.&quot; The conjunction &quot;and&quot; appears in the Hebrew text, but is omitted in the translation for the sake of English style and smoothness. sn The noun מִשְׁפָּט (mishpat, &quot;justice, judgment&quot;) refers to the ability to make a decision that is just (e.g., Deut 16:18; 1 Kgs 3:28). From this legal background, the term came to mean one&apos;s right or precedent. The person with prudence will make decisions that are just and right. 18 sn The Hebrew noun translated &quot;equity&quot; comes from the root יָשָׁר (yashar) which has the basic idea of &quot;upright, straight, right.&quot; It refers to activity that is morally upright and straight, that is, on the proper moral path. Elsewhere it is used in a concrete sense to describe cows walking straight down a path without turning right or left (1 Sam 6:12). Wisdom literature often uses the motif of the straight path to describe a morally &quot;straight&quot; life.

19 tn Heb &quot;to give.&quot; The infinitive construct + ל (lamed) here introduces the fourth purpose of the book: It reveals the purpose from the perspective of the teacher. It is what the wise instructor/sage wants to impart to the naive youths. 20 tn The noun עָרְמָה (&apos;arÿmah) &quot;prudence, shrewdness, craftiness&quot; (BDB 791 s.v.) or &quot;cleverness&quot; (HALOT 886 s.v. 1) refers to a shrewd plan of action, viewed positively or negatively. It is used negatively of planned deception (Josh 9:4) and premeditated murder (Exod 21:14). The related adjective described the serpent as &quot;shrewd, crafty, cunning&quot; (Gen 3:1); it describes cunning plans (Job 5:12) and deception (Job 15:5). The related verb describes a wicked concocted plan (Ps 83:4). The term is used positively of a morally prudent lifestyle (Prov 8:5, 12; 15:5; 19:25). There is no virtue for simpletons to be unaware in this world; they need to be wise as serpents. Proverbs provide a morally shrewd plan for life. 21 tn Heb &quot;the naive&quot; or &quot;simpleton.&quot; The substantival adjective פֶּתִי (peti) means &quot;simple; open-minded&quot; in the sense of being open and easily influenced by either wisdom or folly (BDB 834 s.v.; HALOT 989 s.v. I פֶּתִי). The simpleton is easily enticed and misled (Prov 1:32; 7:7; 9:6; 22:3; 27:12); believes everything, including bad counsel (Prov 14:15); lacks moral prudence (Prov 8:5; 19:25); needs discernment (Prov 21:11); but is capable of learning (Prov 9:4, 16). The related verb means &quot;to be wide open; open-minded; enticed, deceived&quot; (BDB 834). The term describes one easily persuaded and gullible, open to any influence, good or bad (cf. NLT &quot;the simpleminded&quot;). This is the &quot;wide-eyed youth&quot; who is headed for trouble unless he listens to the counsel of wisdom. 22 tn The conjunction &quot;and&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text but is implied; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of smoothness and style. 23 tn Heb &quot;knowledge and purpose.&quot; The noun דַּעַת (da&apos;at, &quot;knowledge&quot;) may be nuanced &quot;discernment&quot; here (HALOT 229 s.v. I דַּעַת 4). The nouns וּמְזִמָּה דַּעַת (da&apos;at umÿzimmah, &quot;discernment and purpose&quot;) form a hendiadys (two nouns joined with vav to describe the same thing): The first noun functions adjectivally and the second functions as a noun: &quot;discerning plan.&quot; This parallels &quot;a shrewd plan for the morally naive&quot; or &quot;a discerning plan for the young person.&quot; 24 tn The noun מְזִמָּה (mÿzimmah) may mean (1) &quot;plan&quot; or (2) &quot;discretion&quot; (BDB 273 s.v.; HALOT 566 s.v.). It describes the ability to make plans or formulate the best course of action for gaining a goal (C. H. Toy, Proverbs [ICC], 7). The related verb זָמַם (zamam) means &quot;to plan; to devise&quot; (BDB 273 s.v.; HALOT 272 s.v. I זמם; e.g., Gen 11:6). Here the nouns &quot;knowledge and plan&quot; (וּמְזִמָּה דַּעַת, da&apos;at umÿzimmah) form a hendiadys: knowledge of how to form and carry out a morally wise plan for life. 25 tn Heb &quot;young man&quot; or &quot;youth.&quot;

26 tn The term &quot;also&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity and smoothness. sn Verse 5 functions as a parenthesis in the purpose statements of 1:1-7. There are two purpose statements in 1:2 (&quot;to know wisdom&quot; and &quot;to discern sayings&quot;). The first is stated in detail in 1:3-4, first from the perspective of the student then the teacher. 1:6 will state the second purpose of 1:2. But between the two the writer notes that even the wise can become wiser. The book is not just for neophytes; it is for all who want to grow in wisdom. 27 tn The verb יִשְׁמַע (yishma&apos;) functions as a jussive of advice or counsel (&quot;Let him hear!&quot;) rather than a customary imperfect (&quot;he will hear&quot;). The jussive is supported by the parallelism with the following Hiphil jussive וְיוֹסֶף (vÿyosef, &quot;Let him add!&quot;). 28 tn Heb &quot;add.&quot; 29 tn The Niphal substantival participle נָבוֹן (navon, &quot;discerning&quot;), rather than the noun, is used to describe a person who is habitually characterized by discernment. 1:5 forms a striking contrast to 1:4 - there was the simpleton and the youth, here the wise and discerning. Both need this book. 30 tn The Hiphil verb וְיוֹסֶף (vÿyosef) is a jussive rather than an imperfect as the final short vowel (segol) and accent on the first syllable shows (BDB 415 s.v. יָסַף Hiph). 31 tn The noun תַּחְבֻּלָה (takhbulah, &quot;direction; counsel&quot;) refers to moral guidance (BDB 287 s.v.). It is related to חֹבֵל (khovel, &quot;sailor&quot;), חִבֵּל (khibel, &quot;mast&quot;) and חֶבֶל (khevel, &quot;rope; cord&quot;), so BDB suggests it originally meant directing a ship by pulling ropes on the mast. It is used in a concrete sense of God directing the path of clouds (Job 37:12) and in a figurative sense of moral guidance (Prov 11:14; 20:18; 24:6). Here it refers to the ability to steer a right course through life (A. Cohen, Proverbs, 2).

32 tn The infinitive construct + ל (lamed) means &quot;to discern&quot; and introduces the fifth purpose of the book. It focuses on the benefits of proverbs from the perspective of the reader. By studying proverbs the reader will discern the hermeneutical key to understanding more and more proverbs. 33 tn The phrase &quot;the meaning of&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 34 tn The noun מְלִיצָה (mÿlitsah) means &quot;allusive expression; enigma&quot; in general, and &quot;proverb, parable&quot; in particular (BDB 539 s.v.; HALOT 590 s.v.). The related noun מֵלִיץ means &quot;interpreter&quot; (Gen 42:23). The related Arabic root means &quot;to turn aside,&quot; so this Hebrew term might refer to a saying that has a &quot;hidden meaning&quot; to its words; see H. N. Richardson, &quot;Some Notes on לִיץ and Its Derivatives,&quot; VT 5 (1955): 163-79. 35 tn This line functions in apposition to the preceding, further explaining the phrase &quot;a proverb and a parable.&quot; 36 tn The term &quot;their&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but seems to be implied; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity and smoothness. 37 tn The noun חִידָה (khidah, &quot;riddle&quot;) designates enigmatic sayings whose meaning is obscure or hidden, such as a riddle (Num 12:8; Judg 14:12, 19), allegory (Ezek 17:2), perplexing moral problem (Pss 49:5; 78:2), perplexing question (1 Kgs 10:1 = 2 Chr 9:1) or ambiguous saying (Dan 8:23); see BDB 295 s.v. and HALOT 309 s.v. If this is related to Arabic hada (&quot;to turn aside, avoid&quot;), it refers to sayings whose meanings are obscure. The sayings of the wise often take the form of riddles that must be discerned.

38 tn Heb &quot;fear of the Lord.&quot; The expression יְהוָה יִרְאַת (yir&apos;at yÿhvah, &quot;fear of Yahweh&quot;) is a genitive-construct in which יְהוָה (&quot;the Lord&quot;) functions as an objective genitive: He is the object of fear. The term יָרַא (yara&apos;) is the common word for fear in the OT and has a basic three-fold range of meanings: (1) &quot;dread; terror&quot; (Deut 1:29; Jonah 1:10), (2) &quot;to stand in awe&quot; (1 Kgs 3:28), (3) &quot;to revere; to respect&quot; (Lev 19:3). With the Lord as the object, it captures the polar opposites of shrinking back in fear and drawing close in awe and adoration. Both categories of meaning appear in Exod 20:20 (where the Lord descended upon Sinai amidst geophysical convulsions); Moses encouraged the Israelites to not be afraid of God arbitrarily striking them dead for no reason (&quot;Do not fear!&quot;) but informed the people that the Lord revealed himself in such a terrifying manner to scare them from sinning (&quot;God has come only to test you and to put the fear of him in you so that you do not sin&quot;). The fear of the Lord is expressed in reverential submission to his will - the characteristic of true worship. The fear of the Lord is the foundation for wisdom (9:10) and the discipline leading to wisdom (15:33). It is expressed in hatred of evil (8:13) and avoidance of sin (16:6), and so results in prolonged life (10:27; 19:23). 39 tn The noun רֵאשִׁית (re&apos;shit) has a two-fold range of meaning (BDB 912 s.v.): (1) &quot;beginning&quot; = first step in a course of action (e.g., Ps 111:10; Prov 17:14; Mic 1:13) or (2) &quot;chief thing&quot; as the principal aspect of something (e.g., Prov 4:7). So fearing the Lord is either (1) the first step in acquiring moral knowledge or (2) the most important aspect of moral knowledge. The first option is preferred because 1:2-6 focuses on the acquisition of wisdom. 40 tn Heb &quot;knowledge.&quot; The noun דָּעַת (da&apos;at, &quot;knowledge&quot;) refers to experiential knowledge, not just cognitive knowledge, including the intellectual assimilation and practical application (BDB 394 s.v.). It is used in parallelism to מוּסָר (musar, &quot;instruction, discipline&quot;) and חָכְמָה (khokhmah, &quot;wisdom, moral skill&quot;). 41 tn The conjunction &quot;but&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the antithetical parallelism. It is supplied in the translation for clarity. 42 tn The term אֱוִיל (&apos;evil, &quot;fool&quot;) refers to a person characterized by moral folly (BDB 17 s.v.). Fools lack understanding (10:21), do not store up knowledge (10:14), fail to attain wisdom (24:7), and refuse correction (15:5; 27:22). They are arrogant (26:5), talk loosely (14:3) and are contentious (20:3). They might have mental intelligence but they are morally foolish. In sum, they are stubborn and &quot;thick-brained&quot; (J. H. Greenstone, Proverbs, 6). 43 tn The verb of בָּזָה (bazah, &quot;despise&quot;) means to treat things of value with contempt, as if they were worthless (BDB 102 s.v.). The classic example is Esau who despised his birthright and sold it for lentil stew (Gen 25:34). The perfect tense of this verb may be classified as characteristic perfect (what they have done and currently do) or gnomic perfect (what they always do in past, present and future). The latter is preferred; this describes a trait of fools, and elsewhere the book says that fools do not change. 44 sn Hebrew word order is emphatic here. Normal word order is: verb + subject + direct object. Here it is: direct object + subject + verb (&quot;wisdom and instruction fools despise&quot;).

45 tn The imperative שְׁמַע (shÿma&apos;, &quot;Listen!&quot;) forms an urgent exhortation which expects immediate compliance with parental instruction. 46 tn Heb &quot;my son.&quot; It is likely that collections of proverbs grew up in the royal courts and were designed for the training of the youthful prince. But once the collection was included in the canon, the term &quot;son&quot; would be expanded to mean a disciple, for all the people were to learn wisdom when young. It would not be limited to sons alone but would include daughters - as the expression &quot;the children of (בְּנֵי, bÿne) Israel&quot; (including males and females) clearly shows. Several passages in the Mishnah and Talmud record instructions to teach daughters the Mosaic law so that they will be righteous and avoid sin as well. The translation &quot;my child,&quot; although not entirely satisfactory, will be used here. 47 tn Heb &quot;training&quot; or &quot;discipline.&quot; See note on 1:2. 48 tn Heb &quot;of.&quot; The noun אָבִיךָ (&apos;avikha, &quot;of your father&quot;) may be classified as a genitive of source. 49 tn Heb &quot;instruction.&quot; In Proverbs the noun תּוֹרַה (torah) often means &quot;instruction&quot; or &quot;moral direction&quot; rather than &quot;law&quot; (BDB 435 s.v. 1.a). It is related to יָרָה (yarah, &quot;to point [or, show] the way&quot; in the Hiphil (BDB 435). Instruction attempts to point a person in the right direction (e.g., Gen 46:28). 50 tn Heb &quot;of.&quot; The noun אִמֶּךָ (&apos;immekha, &quot;of your mother&quot;) may be classified as a genitive of source.

51 tn The comparative &quot;like&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the metaphor; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 52 tn Heb &quot;a garland of grace.&quot; The word חֵן (khen, &quot;grace&quot;) refers to qualities that make a person pleasant and agreeable, e.g., a gracious and charming person (BDB 336 s.v.). The metaphor compares the teachings that produce these qualities to an attractive wreath. 53 tn The noun לִוְיַה (livyah, &quot;wreath; garland&quot;) refers to a headdress and appears only twice in the OT (Prov 1:9; 4:9; BDB 531 s.v.; HALOT 524 s.v.). 54 tn Heb &quot;for.&quot; 55 tn The comparative &quot;like&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the metaphor; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 56 tn Cf. KJV, ASV &quot;chains&quot;; NIV &quot;a chain&quot;; but this English term could suggest a prisoner&apos;s chain to the modern reader rather than adornment. 57 tn Heb &quot;for.&quot;

58 tn The term חַטָּא (khatta&apos;) is the common word for &quot;sinner&quot; in the OT. Because the related verb is used once of sling-shot throwers who miss the mark (Judg 20:16), the idea of sin is often explained as &quot;missing the moral mark&quot; (BDB 306-8 s.v.). But the term should not be restricted to the idea of a sin of ignorance or simply falling short of the moral ideal. Its meaning is more likely seen in the related Akkadian term &quot;to revolt, rebel.&quot; It is active rebellion against authority. It is used here in reference to a gang of robbers. 59 tn The imperfect tense verb יְפַתּוּךָ (yÿftukha) may be nuanced in a connotative sense: &quot;(If) they attempt to persuade you.&quot; The verb פָּתָה (patah) means &quot;to persuade, entice&quot; a person to sin (BDB 834 s.v. פָּתָה 1; see, e.g., Judg 14:15; 16:5; Prov 16:29; Hos 2:16). 60 tc The MT reads the root אָבָה (&apos;avah, &quot;to be willing; to consent&quot;). Some medieval Hebrew mss read the root בּוֹא (bo&apos;, &quot;to go&quot;): &quot;do not go with them.&quot; The majority of Hebrew mss and the versions support the MT reading, which is the less common word and so the more likely original reading.

61 tn This cohortative נֶאֶרְבָה (ne&apos;ervah) could denote resolve (&quot;We will lie in wait!&quot;) or exhortation (&quot;Let us lie in wait!&quot;). These sinners are either expressing their determination to carry out a violent plan or they are trying to entice the lad to participate with them. 62 tn The verb אָרַב (&apos;arav, &quot;to lie in wait&quot;) it is used for planning murder (Deut 19:11), kidnapping (Judg 21:20), or seduction (Prov 23:28). 63 tn Heb &quot;for blood.&quot; The term דָּם (dam, &quot;blood&quot;) functions as a metonymy of effect for &quot;blood shed violently&quot; through murder (HALOT 224 s.v. 4). 64 tn Heb &quot;lie in hiding.&quot; 65 tn The term &quot;innocent&quot; (נָקִי, naqi) intimates that the person to be attacked is harmless. 66 tn Heb &quot;without cause&quot; (so KJV, NASB); NCV &quot;just for fun.&quot; The term חִנָּם (khinnam, &quot;without cause&quot;) emphasizes that the planned attack is completely unwarranted.

67 tn Heb &quot;lives.&quot; The noun חַיִּים (khayyim, &quot;lives&quot;) functions as an adverbial accusative of manner: &quot;alive.&quot; The form is a plural of state, used to describe a condition of life which encompasses a long period of time - in this case a person&apos;s entire life. Murder cuts short a person&apos;s life. 68 tn The noun שְׁאוֹל (shÿ&apos;ol) can mean (1) &quot;death,&quot; cf. NCV; (2) &quot;the grave,&quot; cf. KJV, NIV, NLT (3) &quot;Sheol&quot; as the realm of departed spirits, cf. NAB &quot;the nether world,&quot; and (4) &quot;extreme danger.&quot; Here it is parallel to the noun בוֹר (vor, &quot;the Pit&quot;) so it is the grave or more likely &quot;Sheol&quot; (cf. ASV, NRSV). Elsewhere Sheol is personified as having an insatiable appetite and swallowing people alive as they descend to their death (e.g., Num 16:30, 33; Isa 5:14; Hab 2:5). In ancient Near Eastern literature, the grave is often personified in similar manner, e.g., in Ugaritic mythological texts Mot (= &quot;death&quot;) is referred to as &quot;the great swallower.&quot; 69 tn Heb &quot;and whole.&quot; The vav (ו) is asseverative or appositional (&quot;even&quot;); it is omitted in the translation for the sake of style and smoothness. The substantival adjective תָּמִים (tamim, &quot;whole; perfect; blameless&quot;) is an adverbial accusative describing the condition and state of the object. Used in parallel to חַיִּים (khayyim, &quot;alive&quot;), it must mean &quot;full of health&quot; (BDB 1071 s.v. תָּמִים 2). These cutthroats want to murder a person who is full of vigor.

70 tn Heb &quot;find.&quot; The use of the verb מָצָא (matsa&apos;, &quot;to find&quot;) is deliberate understatement to rhetorically down-play the heinous act of thievery. 71 tn Heb &quot;all wealth of preciousness.&quot; 72 tn The noun שָׁלָל (shalal, &quot;plunder&quot;) functions as an adverbial accusative of material: &quot;with plunder.&quot; This term is normally used for the spoils of war (e.g., Deut 20:14; Josh 7:21; Judg 8:24, 25; 1 Sam 30:20) but here refers to &quot;stolen goods&quot; (so NCV, CEV; e.g., Isa 10:2; Prov 16:19; BDB 1022 s.v. 3). The enticement was to join a criminal gang and adopt a life of crime to enjoy ill-gotten gain (A. Cohen, Proverbs, 4). Cf. NAB, NRSV &quot;booty&quot;; TEV &quot;loot.&quot;

73 tn Heb &quot;Throw in your lot with us.&quot; This is a figurative expression (hypocatastasis) urging the naive to join their life of crime and divide their loot equally. The noun גּוֹרָל (goral, &quot;lot&quot;) can refer to (1) lot thrown for decision-making processes, e.g., choosing the scapegoat (Lev 16:8), discovering a guilty party (Jonah 1:7) or allocating property (Josh 18:6); (2) allotted portion (Josh 15:1) and (3) allotted fate or future destiny (Prov 1:14; Dan 12:13; see BDB 174 s.v.). Here the criminals urged the lad to share their life. The verb תַּפִּיל (tappil) is an imperfect of injunction: &quot;Throw in...!&quot; but might also be an imperfect of permission: &quot;you may throw.&quot; It functions metonymically as an invitation to join their life of crime: &quot;share with us&quot; (BDB 658 s.v. 3). 74 tn Heb &quot;there will be to all of us.&quot; 75 tn Heb &quot;one purse&quot; (so KJV, NAB, NRSV). The term כִּיס (kis, &quot;purse; bag&quot;) is a synecdoche of container (= purse) for contents (= stolen goods). The adjective אֶחָד (&apos;ekhad, &quot;one&quot;) indicates that the thieves promised to share equally in what they had stolen.

76 tn Heb &quot;do not walk.&quot; 77 tn Heb &quot;in the way with them.&quot; 78 tn Heb &quot;your foot.&quot; The term &quot;foot&quot; (רֶגֶל, regel) is a synecdoche of part (= your foot) for the whole person (= yourself). 79 sn The word &quot;path&quot; (נְתִיבָה, nÿtivah) like the word &quot;way&quot; (דֶּרֶךְ, derekh) is used as an idiom (developed from a hypocatastasis), meaning &quot;conduct, course of life.&quot;

80 tn Heb &quot;their feet.&quot; The term &quot;feet&quot; is a synecdoche of the part (= their feet) for the whole person (= they), stressing the eagerness of the robbers. 81 tn Heb &quot;run.&quot; The verb רוּץ (ruts, &quot;run&quot;) functions here as a metonymy of association, meaning &quot;to be eager&quot; to do something (BDB 930 s.v.). 82 tn Heb &quot;to harm.&quot; The noun רַע (ra&apos;) has a four-fold range of meanings: (1) &quot;pain, harm&quot; (Prov 3:30), (2) &quot;calamity, disaster&quot; (13:21), (3) &quot;distress, misery&quot; (14:32) and (4) &quot;moral evil&quot; (8:13; see BDB 948-49 s.v.). The parallelism with &quot;swift to shed blood&quot; suggests it means &quot;to inflict harm, injury.&quot; 83 tn The imperfect tense verbs may be classified as habitual or progressive imperfects describing their ongoing continual activity. 84 tc The BHS editors suggest deleting this entire verse from MT because it does not appear in several versions (Codex B of the LXX, Coptic, Arabic) and is similar to Isa 59:7a. It is possible that it was a scribal gloss (intentional addition) copied into the margin from Isaiah. But this does not adequately explain the differences. It does fit the context well enough to be original.

85 tn Heb &quot;for the net to be spread out.&quot; The Pual participle of זָרָה (zarah) means &quot;to be spread&quot; (HALOT 280 s.v. I זרה pu.1). The subject of this verbal use of the participle is the noun הָרָשֶׁת (harashet, &quot;the net&quot;). It is futile for the net to be spread out in plain view of birds. 86 tn Heb &quot;in the eyes of.&quot; sn This means either: (1) Spreading a net in view of birds is futile because birds will avoid the trap; but the wicked are so blind that they fail to see danger; or (2) it does not matter if a net is spread because birds are so hungry they will eat anyway and be trapped; the wicked act in a similar way. 87 tn Heb &quot;all of the possessors of wings.&quot;

88 sn They think that they are going to shed innocent blood, but in their blindness they do not realize that it is their own blood they shed. Their greed will lead to their destruction. This is an example of ironic poetic justice. They do not intend to destroy themselves; but this is what they accomplish. 89 tn Heb &quot;their own souls.&quot; The term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, &quot;soul&quot;) is used as a metonymy (= soul) of association (= life). The noun נֶפֶשׁ often refers to physical &quot;life&quot; (Exod 21:23; Num 17:3; Judg 5:18; Prov 12:10; BDB 659 s.v. 3.c).

90 tn The exclamation כֵּן (ken, &quot;so; thus; such&quot;) marks a conclusion (BDB 485 s.v.). It draws a comparison between the destruction of the wicked in v. 18 and the concluding statement in v. 19. 91 tc The MT reads אָרְחוֹת (&apos;orkhot, &quot;paths; ways&quot; as figure for mode of life): &quot;so are the ways [or, paths] of all who gain profit unjustly.&quot; The BHS editors suggest emending the text to אַחֲרִית (&apos;akharit, &quot;end&quot; as figure for their fate) by simple metathesis between ח (khet) and ר (resh) and by orthographic confusion between י (yod) and ו (vav), both common scribal errors: &quot;so is the fate of all who gain profit unjustly.&quot; The external evidence supports MT, which is also the more difficult reading. It adequately fits the context which uses &quot;way&quot; and &quot;path&quot; imagery throughout 1:10-19. 92 tn Heb &quot;those who unjustly gain unjust gain.&quot; The participle בֹּצֵעַ (boysea&apos;, &quot;those who unjustly gain&quot;) is followed by the cognate accusative of the same root בָּצַע (batsa&apos;, &quot;unjust gain&quot;) to underscore the idea that they gained their wealth through heinous criminal activity. sn The verb followed by the cognate noun usually means seeking gain in an unjust way (1 Sam 8:3), or for selfish purposes (Gen 37:26), or gaining by violence. The word may have the sense of covetousness. 93 tn The subject of the verb is the noun בָּצַע (&quot;unjust gain&quot;), which is also the referent of the 3rd person masculine singular suffix on בְּעָלָיו (bÿ&apos;alav, &quot;its owners&quot;). Greed takes away the life of those who live by greed (e.g., 15:27; 26:27). See G. R. Driver, &quot;Problems in the Hebrew Text of Proverbs,&quot; Bib 32 (1951): 173-74. 94 tn The term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, &quot;soul&quot;) is used as a metonymy (= soul) of association (= life). The noun נֶפֶשׁ often refers to physical &quot;life&quot; (Exod 21:23; Num 17:3; Judg 5:18; Prov 12:10; BDB 659 s.v. 3.c). 95 tn Heb &quot;its owners.&quot;

96 tn The noun חָכְמָה (khokhmah, &quot;wisdom&quot;) is the abstract feminine plural form. It probably functions as a plural of intensity, stressing the all-embracing, elevated wisdom (W. McKane, Proverbs [OTL], 272). As in 8:1-9:11, Wisdom is personified as a righteous woman in 1:20-33. 97 sn The verb רָנַן (ranan, &quot;to cry out, give a ringing cry&quot;) always expresses excitement, whether of joyful praise or lamentable sorrow (BDB 943 s.v.). Here it is an excited summons. 98 tn Heb &quot;she gives her voice.&quot; The expression means to shout loudly (BDB 679 s.v. נָתַן Qal.x). 99 sn The word רְחֹבוֹת (rÿkhovot, &quot;plazas&quot;) refers to the wide plazas or broad open spaces near the gate where all the people assembled. The personification of wisdom as a woman crying out in this place would be a vivid picture of the public appeal to all who pass by.

100 tc MT reads הֹמִיּוֹת (homyyot, &quot;noisy streets&quot;; Qal participle feminine plural from הָמָה [hamah], &quot;to murmur; to roar&quot;), referring to the busy, bustling place where the street branches off from the gate complex. The LXX reads τειχέων (teicewn) which reflects חֹמוֹת (khomot), &quot;walls&quot; (feminine plural noun from חוֹמָה [khomah], &quot;wall&quot;): &quot;She proclaims on the summits of the walls.&quot; MT is preferred because it is the more difficult form. The LXX textual error was caused by simple omission of yod (י). In addition, the LXX expands the verse to read, &quot;she sits at the gates of the princes, at the gates of the city she boldly says.&quot; The shorter MT reading is preferred. 101 sn The phrase &quot;in the city&quot; further defines the area of the entrance just inside the gate complex, the business area. In an ancient Near Eastern city, business dealings and judicial proceedings would both take place in this area. 102 tn Heb &quot;she speaks her words.&quot;

103 tn Wisdom addresses three types of people: simpletons (פְּתָיִם, pÿtayim), scoffers (לֵצִים, letsim) and fools (כְּסִילִים, kÿsilim). For the term &quot;simpleton&quot; see note on 1:4. Each of these three types of people is satisfied with the life being led and will not listen to reason. See J. A. Emerton, &quot;A Note on the Hebrew Text of Proverbs 1:22-23,&quot; JTS 19 (1968): 609-14. 104 tn Heb &quot;simplicity&quot; (so KJV, NASB); NAB &quot;inanity.&quot; The noun פֶּתִי (peti) means &quot;simplicity; lack of wisdom&quot; (BDB 834 s.v.; HALOT 989 s.v. II פֶּתִי). It is related to the term פְּתָיִם (pÿtayim) &quot;simpletons&quot; and so forms a striking wordplay. This lack of wisdom and moral simplicity is inherent in the character of the naive person. 105 tn The second instance of &quot;How long?&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text; it is supplied in the translation for smoothness and style. 106 sn The term לֵצִים (leysim, &quot;scoffers; mockers&quot;) comes from the root לִיץ (lits, &quot;to scorn; to mock; to speak indirectly&quot; (BDB 539 s.v. לִיץ). They are cynical and defiant freethinkers who ridicule the righteous and all for which they stand (e.g., Ps 1:1). 107 tn Heb &quot;delight.&quot; The verb (חָמַד, khamad) is often translated &quot;to take pleasure; to delight&quot; but frequently has the meaning of a selfish desire, a coveting of something. It is the term, for example, used for coveting in the Decalogue (Exod 20:17; Deut 5:21) and for the covetous desire of Eve (Gen 3:6) and Achan (Josh 7:21). It is tempting to nuance it here as &quot;illicit desire&quot; for mockery. 108 tn Heb &quot;for themselves.&quot; The ethical dative לָהֶם (lahem, &quot;for themselves&quot;) is normally untranslated. It is a rhetorical device emphasizing that they take delight in mockery for their own self-interests. 109 sn The term &quot;fool&quot; (כְּסִיל, kÿsil) refers to the morally insensitive dullard (BDB 493 s.v.).

110 tn The imperfect tense is in the conditional protasis without the conditional particle, followed by the clause beginning with הִנֵּה (hinneh, &quot;then&quot;). The phrase &quot;If only...&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew but is implied by the syntax; it is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 111 tn Heb &quot;turn.&quot; The verb is from שׁוּב (shuv, &quot;to return; to respond; to repent&quot;). 112 sn The noun תּוֹכַחַת (tokhakhat, &quot;rebuke&quot;) is used in all kinds of disputes including rebuking, arguing, reasoning, admonishing, and chiding. The term is broad enough to include here warning and rebuke. Cf. KJV, NAB, NRSV &quot;reproof&quot;; TEV &quot;when I reprimand you&quot;; CEV &quot;correct you.&quot; 113 tn Heb &quot;Behold!&quot; 114 tn The Hiphil cohortative of נָבַע (nava&apos;, &quot;to pour out&quot;) describes the speaker&apos;s resolution to pour out wisdom on those who respond. 115 tn Heb &quot;my spirit.&quot; The term &quot;spirit&quot; (רוּחַ, ruakh) functions as a metonymy (= spirit) of association (= thoughts), as indicated by the parallelism with &quot;my words&quot; (דְּבָרַי, dÿbaray). The noun רוּחַ (ruakh, &quot;spirit&quot;) can have a cognitive nuance, e.g., &quot;spirit of wisdom&quot; (Exod 28:3; Deut 34:9). It is used metonymically for &quot;words&quot; (Job 20:3) and &quot;mind&quot; (Isa 40:13; Ezek 11:5; 20:32; 1 Chr 28:12; see BDB 925 s.v. רוּחַ 6). The &quot;spirit of wisdom&quot; produces skill and capacity necessary for success (Isa 11:2; John 7:37-39). 116 tn The conjunction &quot;and&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for the sake of smoothness. 117 tn Here too the form is the cohortative, stressing the resolution of wisdom to reveal herself to the one who responds.

118 tn The term &quot;however&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the contrast between the offer in 1:23 and the accusation in 1:24-25. It is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 119 tn The particle יַעַן (ya&apos;an, &quot;because&quot;) introduces a causal clause which forms part of an extended protasis; the apodosis is 1:26. 120 tn The phrase &quot;to listen&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew but is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 121 tn The term &quot;because&quot; does not appear in this line but is implied by the parallelism; it is supplied in the translation for clarity and smoothness. 122 sn This expression is a metonymy of adjunct; it is a gesture that goes with the appeal for some to approach.

123 tn Heb &quot;and.&quot; 124 tn The verb III פָּרַע means &quot;to let go; to let alone&quot; (BDB 828 s.v.). It can refer to unkempt hair of the head (Lev 10:6) or lack of moral restraint: &quot;to let things run free&quot; (Exod 32:25; Prov 28:19). Here it means &quot;to avoid, neglect&quot; the offer of wisdom (BDB 829 s.v. 2). 125 tn The verbs are characteristic perfects or indefinite pasts. For the word &quot;comply, consent,&quot; see 1:20.

126 tn The conclusion or apodosis is now introduced. 127 sn Laughing at the consequences of the fool&apos;s rejection of wisdom does convey hardness against the fool; it reveals the folly of rejecting wisdom (e.g., Ps 2:4). It vindicates wisdom and the appropriateness of the disaster (D. Kidner, Proverbs [TOTC], 60). 128 tn Heb &quot;at your disaster.&quot; The 2nd person masculine singular suffix is either (1) a genitive of worth: &quot;the disaster due you&quot; or (2) an objective genitive: &quot;disaster strikes you.&quot; The term &quot;disaster&quot; (אֵיד, &apos;ed) often refers to final life-ending calamity (Prov 6:15; 24:22; BDB 15 s.v. 3). The preposition ב (bet) focuses upon time here. 129 tn Heb &quot;your dread&quot; (so NASB); KJV &quot;your fear&quot;; NRSV &quot;panic.&quot; The 2nd person masculine singular suffix is a subjective genitive: &quot;that which you dread.&quot;

130 tn Heb &quot;your dread.&quot; See note on 1:31. 131 sn The term &quot;whirlwind&quot; (NAB, NIV, NRSV; cf. TEV, NLT &quot;storm&quot;) refers to a devastating storm and is related to the verb שׁוֹא (sho&apos;, &quot;to crash into ruins&quot;; see BDB 996 s.v. שׁוֹאָה). Disaster will come swiftly and crush them like a devastating whirlwind. 132 tn Heb &quot;your disaster.&quot; The 2nd person masculine singular suffix is an objective genitive: &quot;disaster strikes you.&quot; 133 tn Heb &quot;like a storm.&quot; The noun סוּפָה (sufah, &quot;storm&quot;) is often used in similes to describe sudden devastation (Isa 5:28; Hos 8:7; Amos 1:14). 134 tn Heb &quot;distress and trouble.&quot; The nouns &quot;distress and trouble&quot; mean almost the same thing so they may form a hendiadys. The two similar sounding terms צוּקָה (tsuqah) and צָרָה (tsarah) also form a wordplay (paronomasia) which also links them together.

135 tn Heb &quot;look to.&quot; The verb שָׁחַר (shakhar, &quot;to look&quot;) is used figuratively of intensely looking (=seeking) for deliverance out of trouble (W. L. Holladay, Concise Hebrew and Aramaic Lexicon, 366); cf. NLT &quot;anxiously search for.&quot; It is used elsewhere in parallelism with בָּקַשׁ (baqash, &quot;to seek rescue&quot;; Hos 5:15). It does not mean &quot;to seek early&quot; (cf. KJV) as is popularly taught due to etymological connections with the noun שַׁחַר (shakhar, &quot;dawn&quot;; so BDB 1007 s.v. שָׁחַר).

136 tn The causal particle תַּחַת כִּי (takhat ki, &quot;for the reason that&quot;) introduces a second accusation of sin and reason for punishment. 137 tn Heb &quot;knowledge.&quot; The noun דָעַת (da&apos;at, &quot;knowledge&quot;) refers to moral knowledge. See note on 1:7. 138 tn Heb &quot;the fear of the Lord.&quot; The noun is an objective genitive; the Lord is to be the object of fear. See note on 1:7.
139 tn The verb &quot;spurned&quot; (נָאַץ, na&apos;ats) is parallel to &quot;comply, accede to, be willing&quot; (e.g., 1:10). This is how the morally stubborn fool acts (e.g., 15:5).

140 tn The vav (ו) prefixed to the verb וְיֹאכְלוּ (vÿyo&apos;khÿlu) functions in a consecutive logical sense: &quot;therefore.&quot; 141 sn The expression &quot;eat the fruit of&quot; is a figurative expression (hypocatastasis) that compares the consequences of sin to agricultural growth that culminates in produce. They will suffer the consequences of their sinful actions, that is, they will &quot;reap&quot; what they &quot;sow.&quot; 142 sn The words &quot;way&quot; (דֶּרֶךְ, derekh) and &quot;counsel&quot; (מוֹעֵצָה, mo&apos;etsah) stand in strong contrast to the instruction of wisdom which gave counsel and rebuke to encourage a better way. They will bear the consequences of the course they follow and the advice they take (for that wrong advice, e.g., Ps 1:1). 143 tn Heb &quot;to eat to one&apos;s fill.&quot; The verb שָׂבֵעַ (savea&apos;) means (1) positive: &quot;to eat one&apos;s fill&quot; so that one&apos;s appetite is satisfied and (2) negative: &quot;to eat in excess&quot; as a glutton to the point of sickness and revulsion (BDB 959 s.v.). Fools will not only &quot;eat&quot; the fruit of their own way (v. 31a), they will be force-fed this revolting &quot;menu&quot; which will make them want to vomit (v. 31b) and eventually kill them (v. 32).

144 tn Heb &quot;turning away&quot; (so KJV). The term מְשׁוּבַת (mÿshuvat, &quot;turning away&quot;) refers to moral defection and apostasy (BDB 1000 s.v.; cf. ASV &quot;backsliding&quot;). The noun מְשׁוּבַת (&quot;turning away&quot;) which appears at the end of Wisdom&apos;s speech in 1:32 is from the same root as the verb תָּשׁוּבוּ (tashuvu, &quot;turn!&quot;) which appears at the beginning of this speech in 1:23. This repetition of the root שׁוּב (shuv, &quot;to turn&quot;) creates a wordplay: Because fools refuse to &quot;turn to&quot; wisdom (1:23), they will be destroyed by their &quot;turning away&quot; from wisdom (1:32). The wordplay highlights the poetic justice of their judgment. But here they have never embraced the teaching in the first place; so it means turning from the advice as opposed to turning to it. 145 sn The Hebrew verb &quot;to kill&quot; (הָרַג, harag) is the end of the naive who refuse to change. The word is broad enough to include murder, massacre, killing in battle, and execution. Here it is judicial execution by God, using their own foolish choices as the means to ruin. 146 tn Heb &quot;complacency&quot; (so NASB, NIV, NRSV, NLT); NAB &quot;smugness.&quot; The noun שַׁלְוַה (shalvah) means (1) positively: &quot;quietness; peace; ease&quot; and (2) negatively: &quot;self-sufficiency; complacency; careless security&quot; (BDB 1017 s.v.), which is the sense here. It is &quot;repose gained by ignoring or neglecting the serious responsibilities of life&quot; (C. H. Toy, Proverbs [ICC], 29).

147 tn The participle is used substantivally here: &quot;whoever listens&quot; will enjoy the benefits of the instruction. 148 tn The noun בֶּטַח (betakh, &quot;security&quot;) functions as an adverbial accusative of manner: &quot;in security.&quot; The phrase refers to living in a permanent settled condition without fear of danger (e.g., Deut 33:12; Ps 16:9). It is the antithesis of the dread of disaster facing the fool and the simple. 149 tn The verb שַׁאֲנַן (sha&apos;anan) is a Palel perfect of שָׁאַן (sha&apos;an) which means &quot;to be at ease; to rest securely&quot; (BDB 983 s.v. שָׁאַן). Elsewhere it parallels the verb &quot;to be undisturbed&quot; (Jer 30:10), so it means &quot;to rest undisturbed and quiet.&quot; The reduplicated Palel stem stresses the intensity of the idea. The perfect tense functions in the so-called &quot;prophetic perfect&quot; sense, emphasizing the certainty of this blessing for the wise.

1 sn The chapter begins with an admonition to receive wisdom (1-4) and then traces the benefits: the knowledge of God and his protection (5-8), moral discernment for living (9-11), protection from evil men (12-15) and immoral women (16-19), and enablement for righteous living (20-22). 2 tn Heb &quot;my son.&quot; 3 sn Verses 1-11 form one long conditional sentence in the Hebrew text: (1) the protasis (&quot;if...&quot;) encompasses vv. 1-4 and (2) the apodosis (&quot;then...&quot;) consists of two parallel panels in vv. 5-8 and vv. 9-11 both of which are introduced by the particle אָז (&apos;az, &quot;then&quot;). 4 sn The verb &quot;to store up&quot; (צָפַן, tsafan; cf. NAB, NLT &quot;treasure&quot;) in the second colon qualifies the term &quot;receive&quot; (לָקַח, laqakh) in the first, just as &quot;commands&quot; intensifies &quot;words.&quot; This pattern of intensification through parallelism occurs throughout the next three verses. The verb &quot;to store up; to treasure&quot; is used in reference to things of value for future use, e.g., wealth, dowry for a bride. Since proverbs will be useful throughout life and not always immediately applicable, the idea of storing up the sayings is fitting. They will form the way people think which in turn will influence attitudes (W. G. Plaut, Proverbs, 43).

5 tn The Hiphil infinitive construct לְהַקְשִׁיב (lÿhaqshiv, &quot;by making attentive&quot;) functions as an epexegetical explanation of how one will receive the instruction. 6 sn The word &quot;ear&quot; is a metonymy of cause; the word is used as the instrument of hearing. But in parallelism with &quot;heart&quot; it indicates one aspect of the mental process of hearing and understanding. A &quot;hearing ear&quot; describes an obedient or responsive person (BDB 24 s.v. אֹזֶן 2). 7 tn The conjunction &quot;and&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for the sake of smoothness. 8 tn The Hiphil imperfect (&quot;by turning&quot;) continues the nuance introduced by the infinitive construct in the first colon (GKC 352 §114.r). The verb נָטָה (natah) normally means &quot;to stretch out&quot; and only occasionally &quot;to turn&quot; or &quot;to incline&quot; one&apos;s heart to something, as is the case here. 9 tn Or &quot;mind&quot; (the center of the will, the choice).

10 tn Both particles retain their individual meanings, otherwise the verse would begin with a strong adversative and be a contrast to what has been said. 11 tn Heb &quot;summon.&quot; 12 sn The noun recalls the second purpose of the book (1:2). It is also cognate to the last word of 2:2, forming a transition. The two objects of the prepositions in this verse are actually personifications, as if they could be summoned. 13 tn Heb &quot;give your voice&quot;; the expression is idiomatic for raising or lifting the voice to make a sound that carries further (e.g., Jer 2:15). This deliberate expression indicates that something significant is being uttered. J. H. Greenstone says, &quot;If it [understanding] does not come at your first call, raise your voice to a higher pitch, put forth greater efforts&quot; (Proverbs, 17).

1 sn The chapter begins with an introductory exhortation (1-4), followed by an admonition to be faithful to the Lord (5-12). Wisdom is commended as the most valuable possession (13-18), essential to creation (19-20), and the way to a long and safe life (21-26). There then follows a warning to avoid unneighborliness (27-30) and emulating the wicked (31-35). 2 tn Heb &quot;my son&quot; (likewise in vv. 11, 21). 3 tn The verb יִצֹּר (yitsor) is a Qal jussive and the noun לִבֶּךָ (libbekha, &quot;your heart&quot;) functions as the subject: &quot;let your heart keep my commandments.&quot;

4 tn The phrase &quot;they will provide&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but are supplied in the translation for the sake of smoothness. 5 tn Heb &quot;length of days and years of life&quot; (so NASB, NRSV). The idiom &quot;length of days&quot; refers to a prolonged life and &quot;years of life&quot; signifies a long time full of life, a life worth living (T. T. Perowne, Proverbs, 51). The term &quot;life&quot; refers to earthly felicity combined with spiritual blessedness (BDB 313 s.v. חַיִּים). 6 tn The noun שָׁלוֹם (shalom, &quot;peace&quot;) here means &quot;welfare, health, prosperity&quot; (BDB 1022 s.v. 3). It can be used of physical health and personal well-being. It is the experience of positive blessing and freedom from negative harm and catastrophe.

7 tn The two words חֶסֶד וֶאֶמֶת (khesed ve&apos;emet, &quot;mercy and truth&quot;) form a nominal hendiadys, the second word becoming an adjective: &quot;faithful covenant love&quot; or &quot;loyal [covenant] love and faithfulness.&quot; 8 sn This involves two implied comparisons (hypocatastasis). One is a comparison of living out the duties and responsibilities taught with binding a chain around the neck, and the other is a comparison of the inward appropriation of the teachings with writing them on a tablet. So the teachings are not only to become the lifestyle of the disciple but his very nature.

1 sn The chapter includes an exhortation to acquire wisdom (1-4a), a list of the benefits of wisdom (4b-9), a call to pursue a righteous lifestyle (10-13), a warning against a wicked lifestyle (14-19), and an exhortation to righteousness (20-27). 2 tn Heb &quot;sons.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;discipline.&quot; 4 tn The Qal infinitive construct with preposition ל (lamed) indicates the purpose/result of the preceding imperative. 5 tn Heb &quot;know&quot; (so KJV, ASV).

8 tn Or &quot;a boy with my father.&quot; 9 tc The LXX introduces the ideas of &quot;obedient&quot; and &quot;beloved&quot; for these two terms. However, since the image of the adulterous woman probably represents all kinds of folly (through personification), and since even in this particular folly the temptation works both ways, the general address to either young men or women should be retained. 6 sn &quot;Lips&quot; is a metonymy of cause, referring to her words. Dripping honey is an implied comparison between the product and her words, which are flattering and smooth (cf. Song 4:11). 1 sn The chapter advises release from foolish indebtedness (1-5), admonishes avoiding laziness (6-11), warns of the danger of poverty (9-11) and deviousness (12-15), lists conduct that the Lord hates (16-19), and warns about immorality (20-35). 2 tn Heb &quot;my son&quot; (likewise in vv. 3, 20). 3 sn It was fairly common for people to put up some kind of financial security for someone else, that is, to underwrite another&apos;s debts. But the pledge in view here was foolish because the debtor was a neighbor who was not well known (זָר, zar), perhaps a misfit in the community. The one who pledged security for this one was simply gullible. 4 tn The conjunction &quot;and&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is supplied in the translation for the sake of smoothness. 5 tn Heb &quot;struck your hands&quot;; NIV &quot;have struck hands in pledge&quot;; NASB &quot;have given a pledge.&quot; The guarantee of a pledge was signaled by a handshake (e.g., 11:15; 17:18; 22:26). 6 tn Heb &quot;stranger.&quot; The term זוּר (zur, &quot;stranger&quot;) probably refers to a neighbor who was not well-known. Alternatively, it could describe a person who is living outside the norms of convention, a moral misfit in the community. In any case, this &quot;stranger&quot; is a high risk in any financial arrangement.

7 tn The term &quot;if&quot; does not appear in this line but is implied by the parallelism. It is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity. 8 tn The verb יָקַשׁ (yaqash) means &quot;to lay a bait; to lure; to lay snares.&quot; In the Niphal it means &quot;to be caught by bait; to be ensnared&quot; - here in a business entanglement. 9 tn Heb &quot;by the words of your mouth.&quot; The same expression occurs at the end of the following line (cf. KJV, ASV, NASB). Many English versions vary the wording slightly, presumably for stylistic reasons, to avoid redundancy (e.g., NAB, NIV, NRSV, NLT).

10 tn The syntactical construction of imperative followed by an imperative + vav consecutive denotes purpose: &quot;in order to be delivered.&quot; The verb means &quot;to deliver oneself, be delivered&quot; in the Niphal. The image is one of being snatched or plucked quickly out of some danger or trouble, in the sense of a rescue, as in a &quot;brand snatched [Hophal stem] from the fire&quot; (Zech 3:2). 11 tn Heb &quot;have come into the hand of your neighbor&quot; (so NASB; cf. KJV, ASV). The idiom using the &quot;hand&quot; means that the individual has come under the control or the power of someone else. This particular word for hand is used to play ironically on its first occurrence in v. 1. 12 tn In the Hitpael the verb רָפַס (rafas) means &quot;to stamp oneself down&quot; or &quot;to humble oneself&quot; (cf. KJV, NASB, NIV). BDB 952 s.v. Hithp suggests &quot;become a suppliant.&quot; G. R. Driver related it to the Akkadian cognate rapasu, &quot;trample,&quot; and interpreted as trampling oneself, swallowing pride, being unremitting in effort (&quot;Some Hebrew Verbs, Nouns, and Pronouns,&quot; JTS 30 [1929]: 374). 13 tn Heb &quot;be bold.&quot; The verb רָהַב (rahav) means &quot;to act stormily; to act boisterously; to act arrogantly.&quot; The idea here is a strong one: storm against (beset, importune) your neighbor. The meaning is that he should be bold and not take no for an answer. Cf. NIV &quot;press your plea&quot;; TEV &quot;beg him to release you.&quot;

1 sn The chapter begins with the important teaching of the father (1-5), then it focuses on the seduction: first of the victim (6-9), then the temptress (10-12), then the seduction (13-20), and the capitulation (21-23); the chapter concludes with the deadly results of consorting (24-27). 2 tn Heb &quot;my son.&quot; 3 tn Heb &quot;within you&quot; (so NASB, NIV); KJV, ASV, NRSV &quot;with you.&quot; BDB 860 s.v. צָפַן Qal.1 suggests that &quot;within you&quot; means &quot;in your own keeping.&quot;

4 tc Before v. 2 the LXX inserts: &quot;My son, fear the Lord and you will be strong, and besides him, fear no other.&quot; Although this addition has the precedent of 3:7 and 9 and harmonizes with 14:26, it does not fit here; the advice is to listen to the teacher. 5 tn The construction of an imperative with the vav (ו) of sequence after another imperative denotes a logical sequence of purpose or result: &quot;that you may live,&quot; or &quot;and you will live.&quot; 6 tn The term &quot;obey&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew text, but is implied by the parallelism; it is supplied for the sake of clarity and smoothness. Some English versions, in light of the second line of v. 1, supply &quot;guard&quot; (e.g., NIV, NCV, NLT). 7 tn Heb &quot;the little man in your eye.&quot; Traditionally this Hebrew idiom is translated into English as &quot;the apple of your eye&quot; (so KJV, NAB, NIV, NRSV); a more contemporary rendering would be &quot;as your most prized possession.&quot; The word for &quot;man&quot; has the diminutive ending on it. It refers to the pupil, where the object focused on - a man - is reflected in miniature. The point is that the teaching must be the central focus of the disciple&apos;s vision and attention.

8 tn Heb &quot;fingers&quot; (so KJV and many other English versions). In light of Deut 6:8, &quot;fingers&quot; appears to be a metonymy for the lower part of the arm. 9 sn This is an allusion to Deut 6:8. Binding the teachings on the fingers and writing them on the tablets here are implied comparisons for preserving the teaching in memory so that it can be recalled and used with ease.

1 sn In this chapter wisdom is personified. In 1:20-33 wisdom proclaims her value, and in 3:19-26 wisdom is the agent of creation. Such a personification has affinities with the wisdom literature of the ancient Near East, and may have drawn on some of that literature, albeit with appropriate safeguards (Claudia V. Camp, Wisdom and the Feminine in the Book of Proverbs, 23-70). Wisdom in Proverbs 8, however, is not a deity like Egypt&apos;s Ma`at or the Assyrian-Babylonian Ishtar. It is simply presented as if it were a self-conscious divine being distinct but subordinate to God; but in reality it is the personification of the attribute of wisdom displayed by God (R. B. Y. Scott, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes [AB], 69-72; and R. Marcus, &quot;On Biblical Hypostases of Wisdom,&quot; HUCA 23 [1950-1951]: 157-71). Many have equated wisdom in this chapter with Jesus Christ. This connection works only in so far as Jesus reveals the nature of the Father, just as Proverbs presents wisdom as an attribute of God. Jesus&apos; claims included wisdom (Matt 12:42) and a unique knowledge of God (Matt 11:25-27). He even personified wisdom in a way that was similar to Proverbs (Matt 11:19). Paul saw the fulfillment of wisdom in Christ (Col 1:15-20; 2:3) and affirmed that Christ became our wisdom in the crucifixion (1 Cor 1:24, 30). So this personification in Proverbs provides a solid foundation for the similar revelation of wisdom in Christ. But because wisdom is a creation of God in Proverbs 8, it is unlikely that wisdom here is to be identified with Jesus Christ. The chapter unfolds in three cycles: After an introduction (1-3), wisdom makes an invitation (4, 5) and explains that she is noble, just, and true (6-9); she then makes another invitation (10) and explains that she is valuable (11-21); and finally, she tells how she preceded and delights in creation (22-31) before concluding with the third invitation (32-36).

2 tn Heb &quot;head.&quot; The word רֹאשׁ (ro&apos;sh, &quot;head&quot;) refers to the highest area or most important place in the elevated area. The contrast with chapter 7 is striking. There the wayward woman lurked at the corners in the street at night; here wisdom is at the highest point in the open places in view of all. 3 tn Heb &quot;at the house of the paths.&quot; The &quot;house&quot; is not literal here, but refers to where the paths meet (cf. ASV, NIV), that is, the &quot;crossroads&quot; (so NAB, NRSV, NLT).

4 tn Heb &quot;at the mouth of.&quot; 5 tn The cry is a very loud ringing cry that could not be missed. The term רָנַן (ranan) means &quot;to give a ringing cry.&quot; It is often only a shrill sound that might come with a victory in battle, but its use in the psalms for praise shows that it also can have clear verbal content, as it does here. For wisdom to stand in the street and give such a ringing cry would mean that it could be heard by all. It was a proclamation.

1 sn Chapter 9 forms the conclusion of the lengthy introduction to the book. Both wisdom and folly will make their final appeals; and both appeal to the simpletons. Wisdom offers life with no mention of pleasure; folly offers pleasure with no mention of death. The first twelve verses concern accepting wisdom: the invitation of wisdom (1-6), the description of the responses (7-11), and the consequence (12). Verses 13-18 concern accepting folly: the invitation (13-17) and the consequence (18). 2 sn Wisdom is personified as a wise woman. She has prepared a house and established it on seven pillars. This is a reference to the habitable world (e.g., 8:31). For the equation of the house and the world, e.g., 8:29; Job 38:6; and Psalm 104:5 (also G. Boström, Proverbiastudien [LUÅ], 1-14). The &quot;seven pillars&quot; have been variously interpreted, but since seven is a number for completeness and sacredness, the idea seems to be that wisdom produced a perfect world.

3 tn Heb &quot;she has killed her killing.&quot; Cf. KJV &quot;hath killed her beasts&quot;; NAB &quot;has dressed her meat&quot;; NASB &quot;has prepared her food.&quot; 4 sn Wisdom has prepared a sumptuous banquet in this house and sends out her maids to call the simple to come and eat (M. Lichtenstein, &quot;The Banquet Motif in Keret and in Proverbs 9,&quot; JANESCU 1 [1968/69]: 19-31). The figures of meat and wine represent the good teaching of wisdom that will be palatable and profitable (implied comparisons). Compare Isaiah 55:1-2 and John 6:51, 55 for similar uses of the figures. The idea of mixing wine could refer to the practice of mixing wine with spices or with water (as the LXX text assumes; e.g., Prov 23:30; Isa 5:22). Mixed wine was the most intoxicating; thus, her wisdom is attractive. All the imagery lets the simple know that what wisdom has to offer is marvelous.
5 tn The text uses two synonymous terms in construct to express the superlative degree.

1 sn Beginning with ch. 10 there is a difference in the form of the material contained in the book of Proverbs. No longer are there long admonitions, but the actual proverbs, short aphorisms dealing with right or wrong choices. Other than a few similar themes grouped together here and there, there is no arrangement to the material as a whole. It is a long collection of approximately 400 proverbs. 2 tn Heb &quot;son.&quot; 3 tn The imperfect tense describes progressive or habitual action, translated here with an English present tense. These fit the nature of proverbs which are general maxims, and not necessarily absolutes or universal truths. One may normally expect to find what the proverb notes, and one should live according to its instructions in the light of those expectations; but one should not be surprised if from time to time there is an exception. The fact that there may be an exception does not diminish the need to live by the sayings. 4 tn Heb &quot;son.&quot; 5 tn Heb &quot;grief of his mother.&quot; The noun &quot;grief&quot; is in construct, and &quot;mother&quot; is an objective genitive. The saying declares that the consequences of wisdom or folly affects the parents.

6 tn Heb &quot;treasures of wickedness&quot; (so KJV, ASV); NASB &quot;Ill-gotten gains&quot;; TEV &quot;Wealth that you get by dishonesty.&quot; 7 sn The term &quot;righteousness&quot; here means honesty (cf. TEV). Wealth has limited value even if gained honestly; but honesty delivers from mortal danger. 8 tn Heb &quot;death.&quot; This could refer to literal death, but it is probably figurative here for mortal danger or ruin.

9 tn Heb &quot;does not allow...to go hungry.&quot; The expression &quot;The Lord does not allow the appetite of the righteous to go hungry&quot; is an example of tapeinosis - a figurative expression stated in the negative to emphasize the positive: The Lord satisfies the appetite of the righteous. 10 tn The term נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh) means &quot;soul&quot; but its root meaning is &quot;throat&quot; and it has a broad range of meanings; here it denotes &quot;appetite&quot; (BDB 660 s.v. 5.a; see, e.g., Pss 63:6; 107:9; Prov 27:7; Isa 56:11; 58:10; Jer 50:19; Ezek 7:19). The term could denote &quot;desire&quot; (BDB 660 s.v. 6.a) which would include the inner urge for success. By contrast, the wicked live unfulfilled lives - as far as spiritual values are concerned. 11 tn Heb &quot;thrusts away&quot; (cf. ASV, NASB); NLT &quot;refuses to satisfy.&quot; The verb הָדַף (hadaf) means &quot;to thrust away; to push; to drive,&quot; either to depose or reject (BDB 213 s.v.). 12 tn This verse contrasts the &quot;appetite&quot; of the righteous with the &quot;craving&quot; of the wicked. This word הַוַּה (havvah, &quot;craving&quot;) means &quot;desire&quot; often in a bad sense, as &apos;the desire of the wicked,&quot; which could not be wholesome (Ps 52:9).

1 tn Heb &quot;an abomination of the Lord.&quot; The term יְהוָה (yÿhvah, &quot;the Lord&quot;) is a subjective genitive. 2 tn Heb &quot;scales of deception.&quot; The genitive is attributive: &quot;deceptive scales.&quot; This refers to dishonesty in the market where silver was weighed in the scales. God condemns dishonest business practices (Deut 25:13-16; Lev 10:35-36), as did the ancient Near East (ANET 388, 423). 3 tn Heb &quot;a perfect stone.&quot; Stones were used for measuring amounts of silver on the scales; here the stone that pleases the Lord is whole, complete, perfect (from שָׁלֵם, shalem). It was one that would give an honest, accurate measurement.

4 tn Heb &quot;presumptuousness.&quot; This term is from the root זִיד, zid (or זוּד, zud) which means &quot;to boil; to seethe; to act proudly; to act presumptuously.&quot; The idea is that of boiling over the edge of the pot, signifying overstepping the boundaries (e.g., Gen 25:29). 5 tn The verbs show both the sequence and the correlation. The first is the perfect tense of בּוֹא (bo&apos;, &quot;to enter; to come&quot;); it is followed by the preterite with vav consecutive from the same verb, showing that one follows or comes with the other. Because the second verb in the colon is sequential to the first, the first may be subordinated as a temporal clause. 6 sn This proverb does not state how the disgrace will come, but affirms that it will follow pride. The proud will be brought down. 7 tn Heb &quot;modesty&quot;; KJV, ASV &quot;the lowly.&quot; The adjective צְנוּעִים (tsÿnu&apos;im, &quot;modest&quot;) is used as a noun; this is an example of antimeria in which one part of speech is used in the place of another (see E. W. Bullinger, Figures of Speech, 491-506), e.g., &quot;Let the dry [adjective] appear!&quot; = dry land (Gen 1:9). The root צָנַע (tsana&apos;, &quot;to be modest; to be humble&quot;) describes those who are reserved, retiring, modest. The plural form is used for the abstract idea of humility. 8 tn The term &quot;comes&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew, but is supplied in the translation from parallelism.

9 sn This contrasts two lifestyles, affirming the value of integrity. The upright live with integrity - blamelessness - and that integrity leads them in success and happiness. Those who use treachery will be destroyed by it. 10 tc The form is a Kethib/Qere reading. The Qere יְשָׁדֵּם (yÿshadem) is an imperfect tense with the pronominal suffix. The Kethib וְשַׁדָּם (vÿshadam) is a perfect tense with a vav prefixed and a pronominal suffix. The Qere is supported by the versions.

1 tn The term &quot;accepts&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew but is supplied in the translation for the sake of smoothness and clarity. 2 tc G. R. Driver suggested reading this word as מְיֻסַּר (mÿyussar, &quot;allows himself to be disciplined&quot;); see his &quot;Hebrew Notes on Prophets and Proverbs,&quot; JTS 41 (1940): 174. But this is not necessary at all; the MT makes good sense as it stands. Similarly, the LXX has &quot;a wise son listens to his father.&quot; tn Heb &quot;discipline of a father.&quot; 3 sn The &quot;scoffer&quot; is the worst kind of fool. He has no respect for authority, reviles worship of God, and is unteachable because he thinks he knows it all. The change to a stronger word in the second colon - &quot;rebuke&quot; (גָּעַר, ga&apos;ar) - shows that he does not respond to instruction on any level. Cf. NLT &quot;a young mocker,&quot; taking this to refer to the opposite of the &quot;wise son&quot; in the first colon.

4 tn Heb &quot;lips&quot; (so NIV); KJV &quot;mouth.&quot; The term &quot;lips&quot; is a metonymy of cause for what the lips produce: speech. 5 tn Heb &quot;he eats [what is] good.&quot; 6 tn Heb &quot;the desire of the faithless.&quot; The noun &quot;faithless&quot; is a subjective genitive: &quot;the faithless desire....&quot; 7 tn The noun נֶפֶשׁ (nefesh, traditionally &quot;soul&quot;) has a broad range of meanings, and here denotes &quot;appetite&quot; (e.g., Ps 17:9; Prov 23:3; Eccl 2:24; Isa 5:14; Hab 2:5; BDB 660 s.v. 5.c) or (2) &quot;desire&quot; (e.g., Deut 12:20; Prov 13:4; 19:8; 21:10; BDB 660 s.v. 6.a). 8 tn Heb &quot;violence.&quot; The phrase &quot;the fruit of&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew but is implied by the parallelism. The term &quot;violence&quot; is probably a metonymy of cause: &quot;violence&quot; represents what violence gains - ill-gotten gains resulting from violent crime. The wicked desire what does not belong to them. tc The LXX reads &quot;the souls of the wicked perish untimely.&quot; The MT makes sense as it stands.

9 tn Heb &quot;mouth&quot; (so KJV, NAB). The term פֶּה (peh, &quot;mouth&quot;) functions as a metonymy of cause for speech. 10 tn The term &quot;but&quot; does not appear in the Hebrew but is supplied in the translation for the sake of clarity and smoothness. 11 tn Heb &quot;opens wide his lips.&quot; This is an idiom meaning &quot;to be talkative&quot; (BDB 832 s.v. פָּשַׂק Qal). Cf. NIV &quot;speaks rashly&quot;; TEV &quot;a careless talker&quot;; CEV &quot;talk too much.&quot; 12 sn Tight control over what one says prevents trouble (e.g., Prov 10:10; 17:28; Jas 3:1-12; Sir 28:25). Amenemope advises to &quot;sleep a night before speaking&quot; (5:15; ANET 422, n. 10). The old Arab proverb is appropriate: &quot;Take heed that your tongue does not cut your throat&quot; (O. Zockler, Proverbs, 134).

1 tn Heb &quot;wise ones of women.&quot; The construct phrase חַכְמוֹת נָשִׁים (khakhmot nashim) features a wholistic genitive: &quot;wise women.&quot; The plural functions in a distributive sense: &quot;every wise woman.&quot; The contrast is between wise and foolish women (e.g., Prov 7:10-23; 31:10-31). 2 tn The perfect tense verb in the first colon functions in a gnomic sense, while the imperfect tense in the second colon is a habitual imperfect. 3 tn Heb &quot;house.&quot; This term functions as a synecdoche of container (= house) for contents (= household, family).

4 tn Heb &quot;fear of the Lord.&quot; The term יְהוָה (yÿhvah, &quot;the Lord&quot;) functions as an objective genitive. 5 tn Heb &quot;crooked of ways&quot;; NRSV &quot;devious in conduct.&quot; This construct phrase features a genitive of specification: &quot;crooked in reference to his ways.&quot; The term &quot;ways&quot; is an idiom for moral conduct. The evidence that people fear the Lord is uprightness; the evidence of those who despise him is the devious ways.

6 tn The preposition בְּ (bet) may denote (1) exchange: &quot;in exchange for&quot; foolish talk there is a rod; or (2) cause: &quot;because of&quot; foolish talk. 7 sn The noun פֶּה (peh, &quot;mouth&quot;) functions as a metonymy of cause for what is said (&quot;speech, words, talk&quot;). 8 tc The MT reads גַּאֲוָה (ga&apos;avah, &quot;pride&quot;) which creates an awkward sense &quot;in the mouth of a fool is a rod of pride&quot; (cf. KJV, ASV). The BHS editors suggest emending the form to גֵּוֹה (&quot;disciplining-rod&quot;) to create tighter parallelism and irony: &quot;in the mouth of a fool is a rod for the back&quot; (e.g., Prov 10:13). What the fools says will bring discipline. tn Heb &quot;a rod of back.&quot; The noun גֵּוֹה functions as a genitive of specification: &quot;a rod for his back.&quot; The fool is punished because of what he says. 9 tn Heb &quot;lips.&quot; The term &quot;lips&quot; is a metonymy of cause, meaning what they say. The wise by their speech will find protection.

1 tn Heb &quot;plans of the heart&quot; (so ASV, NASB, NIV). The phrase מַעַרְכֵי־לֵב (ma&apos;arkhe-lev) means &quot;the arrangements of the mind.&quot; sn Humans may set things in order, plan out what they are going to say, but God sovereignly enables them to put their thoughts into words. 2 tn Heb &quot;[are] to a man.&quot; 3 tn Here &quot;the tongue&quot; is a metonymy of cause in which the instrument of speech is put for what is said: the answer expressed. 4 sn The contrasting prepositions enhance the contrasting ideas - the ideas belong to people, but the words come from the Lord. 5 sn There are two ways this statement can be taken: (1) what one intends to say and what one actually says are the same, or (2) what one actually says differs from what the person intended to say. The second view fits the contrast better. The proverb then is giving a glimpse of how God even confounds the wise. When someone is trying to speak [&quot;answer&quot; in the book seems to refer to a verbal answer] before others, the Lord directs the words according to his sovereign will.

6 tn Heb &quot;ways of a man.&quot; 7 sn The Hebrew term translated &quot;right&quot; (z~E) means &quot;innocent&quot; (NIV) or &quot;pure&quot; (NAB, NRSV, NLT). It is used in the Bible for pure oils or undiluted liquids; here it means unmixed actions. Therefore on the one hand people rather naively conclude that their actions are fine. 8 tn Heb &quot;in his eyes.&quot; 9 tn The figure (a hypocatastasis) of &quot;weighing&quot; signifies &quot;evaluation&quot; (e.g., Exod 5:8; 1 Sam 2:3; 16:7; Prov 21:2; 24:12). There may be an allusion to the Egyptian belief of weighing the heart after death to determine righteousness. But in Hebrew thought it is an ongoing evaluation as well, not merely an evaluation after death. 10 tn Heb &quot;spirits&quot; (so KJV, ASV). This is a metonymy for the motives, the intentions of the heart (e.g., 21:2 and 24:2). sn Humans deceive themselves rather easily and so appear righteous in their own eyes; but the proverb says that God evaluates motives and so he alone can determine if the person&apos;s ways are innocent.

11 tc The MT reads גֹּל (gol, &quot;commit&quot;) from the root גָּלַל (galal, &quot;to roll&quot;). The LXX and Tg. Prov 16:3 have &quot;reveal&quot; as if the root were גָּלָה (galah, &quot;to reveal&quot;). tn Heb &quot;roll.&quot; The verb גֹּל (&quot;to commit&quot;) is from the root גָּלַל (&quot;to roll&quot;). The figure of rolling (an implied comparison or hypocatastasis), as in rolling one&apos;s burdens on the Lord, is found also in Pss 22:8 [9]; 37:5; and 55:22. It portrays complete dependence on the Lord. This would be accomplished with a spirit of humility and by means of diligent prayer, but the plan must also have God&apos;s approval. 12 tn The suffix on the plural noun would be a subjective genitive: &quot;the works you are doing,&quot; or here, &quot;the works that you want to do.&quot; 13 tn The syntax of the second clause shows that there is subordination: The vav on וְיִכֹּנוּ (vÿyikonu) coming after the imperative of the first clause expresses that this clause is the purpose or result. People should commit their works in order that the Lord may establish them. J. H. Greenstone says, &quot;True faith relieves much anxiety and smoothens many perplexities&quot; (Proverbs, 172).
